name: Bobby Witt Jr.
season_outlook: Witt followed up his sizzling, 2023 second-half breakthrough with a 2024 that might have garnered him an MVP award (not to mention top placement on our fantasy leaderboards), if not for Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge. Witt became the first player to manage multiple 30/30 seasons before his 25th birthday, and the 11th shortstop of any age with a 30/30 campaign. He led the majors in batting average, and was one of only six players with at least 100 runs scored and 100 RBI. Witt is one of the game's few true five-category rotisserie superstars, his combination of solid contact and extra-base ability affording him the chance to challenge for the fantasy points leaderboard. Plus, he's still only 24 years old. If there's a nit to pick, it's that he attempted only 15 steals across his most recent 94 games (playoffs included), which could be as much small sample size noise as it might signal his seeing more red lights on the bases as his bat becomes more critical to the Royals' competitive chances.

name: Jose Ramirez
season_outlook: A consistently excellent all-around player despite playing under a relatively small spotlight in Cleveland, Ramirez should be a first-round pick in fantasy leagues of all types. He's the only player to have finished among the top 25 on our Player Rater as well as in total fantasy points scored in each of the past five seasons. In four of those, he finished among the top eight in each, and across that five-year span his 2,118 fantasy points were second only to Shohei Ohtani's 3,151. What's more, in 2024, Ramirez finished just one home run shy of becoming the second-oldest member of the 40/40 club (Barry Bonds, age 31, 1996), a signal that he still has plenty to offer fantasy managers. He's among the safest investments you'll find.

name: Francisco Lindor
season_outlook: After a sluggish start to his Mets career, Lindor has recaptured his form as one of baseball's best all-around players. He has managed at least 31 home runs, 91 RBI, 29 stolen bases and 107 runs scored in both of the last two seasons, and showed decidedly improved raw power metrics. In fact, Lindor's strong finish to 2024 -- he hit .306/.368/.575 with 16 homers after the All-Star break -- hints at a possibly larger step forward in 2025. As the Mets made a big splash in free agency -- some guy named Soto -- Lindor's surging metrics come at an opportune time, as the team's offense should enjoy a noticeable boost from top to bottom. Lindor is a top-25 overall pick who, with some good fortune, could deliver first-round fantasy production.

name: Shohei Ohtani
season_outlook: Ohtani has scripted quite the résumé already over his seven MLB seasons: Rookie of the Year (2018), MVP honors (2021), first player in history to hit 30-plus homers while also striking out 200-plus batters (2022), back-to-back MVPs (2023-24) and, most recently, becoming the charter member of baseball's 50/50 club (2024). While further history book rewrites might seem logically unattainable for the now-30-year-old, it's still within the realm of possibility that he'll score a career-high total fantasy points in 2025 and/or set a personal best in Wins Above Replacement. As both a hitter and pitcher from 2021-23 -- his expected role once again in 2025 -- Ohtani averaged 214 fantasy points more than the league's next-best player annually, an advantage that can be readily exploited in ESPN's standard game with its daily transaction format. Ohtani's fantasy utility hinges heavily upon how your league handles him, but a universal, No. 1 overall case is a relatively easy one.

name: Aaron Judge
season_outlook: What toe problem? Judge, who missed 42 games after tearing a ligament in his right big toe crashing into an outfield wall in June 2023, entered 2024 facing legitimate questions about future maintenance of the ailment. Instead, he delivered a season for the ages: MLB-leading numbers in home runs, RBIs, walks (133), OBP (.458), slugging (.701), OPS (1.159), OPS-plus (223) and Wins Above Replacement (10.8). Oh, yes, and a career-high 158 games played. Judge's contact-quality metrics are off the charts -- he has paced the majors in expected wOBA, Barrel and hard-hit rates among hitters with at least as many plate appearances as his in each of the past three seasons -- and he's among the game's most selective hitters, even if his game has lots of swing-and-miss. There aren't many more well-rounded players to select with a first-round fantasy draft pick.

name: Pete Alonso
season_outlook: Alonso is 30, coming off a season with a career-high 42% ground-ball rate, and his free agency lingered deep into the offseason. All of this spawns concerns about his fantasy value that hadn't previously been present. He remains one of the game's premier power sources, hitting 34 home runs in 2024, making him the only player with at least that many in each of the past five full MLB seasons, but other aspects of his game have begun trending in the wrong direction. In the right environment, Alonso might yet have more seasons within range of his 2022-23 output in his bat, but his downside is beginning to deepen. Consider him to be an early- to mid-round pick, but he's no longer the fantasy building block he once was.

name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
season_outlook: Although his six-year MLB career hasn't yet reached the stratospheric levels that his Hall of Fame father's did, Junior has had some impressive exploits in his own right. Guerrero's 2024 saw him set personal bests in batting average, doubles, contact and whiff rates. It was his third 30-HR campaign and the fourth year in a row with at least 94 RBI. His contact-quality metrics rate among the best in the game, as his Statcast expected batting average across the past four seasons (.303) is fifth-best (minimum 1,200 plate appearances). Plus, he has played in all but 12 Blue Jays games during that time. The primary thing holding Guerrero back from an early first-round valuation is his ground ball-oriented swing. If he could once again show the kind of lift he did during his 48-HR 2021, he'd contend for an MVP award.

name: Ketel Marte
season_outlook: Only a left ankle sprain which cost him three weeks in late August/early September stood in Marte's way towards cementing his status as one of fantasy baseball's most productive hitters, but perhaps that missed time (and how it influences the perception of his worth) will merely serve to keep him affordable come draft day. He set personal bests with his 36 home runs and 95 RBI, fully supported by huge spikes in contact quality. His hard-hit rate was 14% greater than his career number in the category and he made huge strides defensively at second base. For you daily-transactions folks, bear in mind that his .414 wOBA against left-handed pitchers over the past five seasons is third-best in baseball (minimum 150 plate appearances). Consider taking Marte, a top-25 performer in both fantasy points and on our Player Rater last year, in the opening rounds of any draft.

name: Juan Soto
season_outlook: The Mets have given Soto's fantasy managers 765 million reasons to trust in his elite talent. He's one of six players in history to register a .400 OBP in each of his first seven seasons, and one of three from that group (Ted Williams, Frank Thomas) to also manage at least a 140 OPS-plus in each year. Soto's 201 career home runs before turning 26 are also tied for sixth-most in history, and he's the only player to register a top-15 fantasy point total among hitters in each of the past six seasons. He is the epitome of the high-floor, safe return on investment first-round pick, even if his profit potential is greater in leagues that reward his patience. Nevertheless, Soto could be headed for a prime-years uptick, playing the 2025 season at the age of 26.

name: Cal Raleigh
season_outlook: Raleigh set new personal bests with 34 home runs and 100 RBI last season, finishing as the No. 2 catcher in traditional fantasy leagues despite a .220 batting average. The switch-hitting backstop has become a folk hero of sorts in Seattle with his majestic homers and timely hitting among other reasons. The fact that he's a significant plus behind the plate with his defense and framing helps Raleigh's chances of approaching or exceeding 600 plate appearances for the Mariners once again in 2025. The drain in batting average is significant but does not negate the value of his power and counting stats, which get a scarcity bump in two-catcher formats. Expect more of the same in 2025 with Raleigh overcoming the pitcher-friendly skew of his home ballpark.

name: Corbin Carroll
season_outlook: Fresh off his unanimous 2023 NL Rookie of the Year campaign -- one that saw him become the first rookie in baseball history with at least 25 home runs and 50 stolen bases -- Carroll spent the first half of 2024 making a compelling case for fantasy bust of the year. A near-universal first round pick, he entered the All-Star break batting just .213 with five home runs, three of which came in the eight days leading into it, as he struggled throughout to adapt to swing changes he had implemented the prior winter. Carroll finally got it together during the second half, hitting .259/.351/.568 with 17 homers and 17 steals in 64 games, a welcome sign that the rotisserie superstar of old had returned. Just 24, Carroll would surely benefit from better luck on balls in play, but all signs have him returning to near top-10 form in 2025. It's just a year too late for those who drafted him that way last spring.

name: Freddie Freeman
season_outlook: A model of consistency for more than a decade, Freeman has scored 400-plus fantasy points in eight of his 14 full MLB seasons, matching Mike Trout for the most by any player during that time span, while finishing among the top-25 overall on the Player Rater in five of the past seven years. Freeman's combination of polished approach at the plate and elite quality of contact makes him one of the highest-floor players in fantasy baseball, even as his age-35 season dawns. Sure, his so-so second half -- his .790 OPS after the All-Star break was his worst in any half-season since 2015's second half -- beckons questions about the aging curve, and the ankle injury that bothered him late in the year (and in the postseason) which required December surgery warrants a spring check-in. That said, Freeman is otherwise a rock-solid, foundational piece to select in your draft's opening rounds.

name: Manny Machado
season_outlook: While not a lock, Machado might very well be headed to Cooperstown one day, and he continued to produce at a high level in 2024. The third baseman smacked 29 homers and finished third in the National League with 105 RBI, marking the third time he's cleared the century mark in the last four seasons. Machado's OBP has dipped in recent years as his patience has waned, but he continues to hit the ball hard and remains a model of good health, clearing 600 plate appearances in each of the last nine full MLB seasons. He endured a rough month of May and grounded into 25 double plays last year, most in the majors, which speaks to his reduced mobility at 32 years old. Perhaps he will be a bit more susceptible to streakiness moving forward, but for now, Machado can still be a viewed as a foundational piece of any fantasy offense.

name: Elly De La Cruz
season_outlook: One of the game's most fun, dynamic young talents, De La Cruz burst forth with a historic, breakthrough 2024 that probably didn't even garner the level of attention it deserved. He managed only the seventh season of at least 25 home runs and 60 stolen bases in history, while becoming only the eight different shortstop ever to play at least 160 games at the position while delivering at least 70 extra-base hits. Sure, De La Cruz struck out a ton (an MLB-leading 218 times), as scouts hinted he might, but his excellent raw metrics (contact quality, bat speed, sprint speed) and 23 years of age suggest he has room to grow all-around. It's easy to formulate a first-round case for him in rotisserie leagues, and points-league managers should keep in mind that he finished 47th overall in scoring despite all those K's.

name: Bryce Harper
season_outlook: When the curtain closes on Harper's career, he's going to go down as one of the all-time greats, even if during its course it felt like he sometimes fell shy of expectations. Across just the past 10 seasons, Harper has five seasons of 30-plus homers, six of at least a .280 batting average, and five with at least a .900 OPS. The only other player who can make that same claim during that time span is Mike Trout. Now 32, Harper continues to possess elite contact and a patient approach, meaning he should have a few more solid fantasy seasons ahead of him. That he bats in the heart of a still-productive Phillies lineup, in their homer-friendly venue, certainly helps his early-round valuation.

name: Rafael Devers
season_outlook: Devers is one of the game's more underappreciated raw power sources, probably in large part because he has never even placed among the top 10 in MVP balloting across eight MLB seasons. Nevertheless, he's the only hitter who can claim at least 30 doubles, 25 homers and a .500 slugging percentage in each of the past four seasons, during which time his Statcast average exit velocities and hard-hit rates have all rated in at least the 92nd percentile. Remarkably, Devers can claim that despite having been hampered by shoulder issues that cost him 11 of Boston's final 31 games and caused him to hit just .177 with one extra-base hit (a double) in the other 19. With a clean bill of health during spring training, he could be primed for a return to the 35-HR plateau. Draft him accordingly.

name: Kyle Tucker
season_outlook: A shin contusion that later revealed a small fracture, costing the right fielder 79 games, might be the one thing holding Tucker back from entering 2025 as one of fantasy baseball's most prominent superstars. At the time of the injury, caused by his fouling a pitch off his shin, he was on pace for a 50/27 season and 112 runs scored, continuing his pattern as one of baseball's most reliable five-category rotisserie performers. Tucker returned in September with a flourish, batting .365 with four homers across 18 games, giving confidence that he should resume in 2025 where he left off in his walk year with his new team, the Cubs. In fact, he might have room to grow, considering 2024 saw him set new personal bests with his 16.5% walk, 17.5% chase, 41.3% fly ball and 12.9% Barrel rates.

name: Mookie Betts
season_outlook: A paragon of fantasy baseball excellence across the past nine seasons, Betts has hit .294 while averaging 30 home runs, 88 RBI, 19 stolen bases, 113 runs scored and 503 fantasy points per 162 team games over that time. His cumulative numbers in those categories rank ninth (minimum 2,000 plate appearances), seventh, ninth, ninth, first and second overall. Additionally, he entered both 2024 (OF/2B) and 2025 (OF/SS) with dual-positional eligibility and added additional eligibility in-season in 2023 (2B, SS) and 2024 (SS). Even at 32 years old, Betts appears primed for another year of steady, first round-caliber production, in large part due to his elite plate discipline and positioning atop the productive Dodgers lineup, one of the most fantasy-friendly roles in the league.

name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
season_outlook: Tatis was limited to 102 games last season due to a stress reaction in his right femur. His production was an improvement over a down 2023 season, but it fell short of the lofty standards established over the first three years of his career. The main difference was a drop in power fueled by a slightly lower average exit velocity on flyballs, though his barrel rate was still 92nd percentile. Tatis ran less last season with only 11 steals in 14 tries, though it is encouraging that he was 3-for-3 in September after returning from the leg injury. After he stole a total of 54 bases on 62 attempts over his two seasons prior to last, it's reasonable to expect more running this season, putting the 26-year-old in the first-round discussion.

name: Ronald Acuna Jr.
season_outlook: Acuna's seven-year MLB career has been quite the rollercoaster ride. He has won NL Rookie of the Year (2018) and MVP Awards (2023). He's had a 41/37 campaign (2019) and the majors' first-ever 40/70 season (2023) on his résumé, yet has also dealt with three separate ACL injuries (among other ailments) including surgeries on both of his knees (the right in 2021, the left in 2024). Fantasy managers should heed Acuna's performance initially returning from surgery the last time, as he missed the first three weeks of 2022 while recovering, then finished 65th on the Player Rater and tied for 175th in fantasy points scored. A sluggish start could be his downside -- tuck that away as a strategic nugget to perhaps instead trade for him in-season -- but his upside remains that of a five-category rotisserie superstar. If reports on his health during spring training look good, he shouldn't slide much further than the first couple of rounds of rotisserie drafts, nor far outside the top-25 overall in points leagues.

name: Kyle Schwarber
season_outlook: Be it by design or happenstance, Schwarber's groundball rate last year was his highest in a full season since 2018. Coupled with a career-high hard-hit rate on grounders, Schwarber posted the second-best batting average of his career. His power dipped, but Schwarber's 38 homers were still the eighth most in MLB last season and his quality of contact remained elite. The overall improvement stemmed from hitting southpaws better than right-handers for the first time in his career. Splits like this are often anomalies, so expect regression as Schwarber's platoon splits likely revert to career levels. Keep in mind too that drafting Schwarber means locking up the utility spot since he has lost outfield eligibility entering 2025.

name: Cody Bellinger
season_outlook: The Yankees' big hitting acquisition following Juan Soto's free-agent departure, Bellinger brings his pull-power, fly ball-oriented swing to Yankee Stadium -- possibly the best fit yet for his skill set. Though Bellinger's contact-quality metrics have been below-average for four years running, he gets the most out of his swings, and his improved contact over the last two seasons gives him as much of a chance at contributing batting average as well as home runs. A rebound to his 2023 norms might be a stretch, but it's not entirely out of the question in pinstripes. He's well worth a mid-round selection.

name: Julio Rodriguez
season_outlook: Here's one of the most disappointing players of 2024, as his ADP in ESPN leagues was 18th overall, but he finished 55th on the Player Rater and tied for 170th in fantasy points. Rodriguez, only 24, has plenty of time to straighten things out.  Besides, his season wasn't a complete catastrophe, as he joined Mike Trout and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only three players in history to manage 20/20 numbers in each of their first three full MLB seasons. He also maintained strong underlying metrics in terms of his contact quality and raw speed, and he managed .295/.345/.486 rates, nine home runs and six stolen bases across his final 43 games after returning from a mid-year ankle injury. Rodriguez remains one of the game's most talented young players, albeit one who has shown a tendency for slow starts and is more of a rotisserie than points-based prospective star. He remains a strong early-round pick, especially in roto.

name: Matt Olson
season_outlook: Olson was not exempt from the seemingly team-wide funk that struck the 2024 Braves. He posted his worst OPS and OPS-plus as well as his worst strikeout, walk, home run, hard-hit and Statcast Barrel rates since the abbreviated 2020 campaign, although his cumulative numbers wound up looking eerily similar to his 2022 effort. His 2024 looked unusually unlucky and the fact he finished the year on a .282/.380/.573, 16-HR flourish across the Braves' final 60 games suggests that he'll rebound to a degree. Olson was effectively a top-40 overall player in points leagues and a top-70 rotisserie perforner in 2021-22, which seems like a fair valuation for what to expect from him in 2025.

name: Steven Kwan
season_outlook: Few players possess Kwan's elite level of bat control, as evidenced by his 88.9% contact and 28.1% line-drive rates across his three MLB seasons, second- and eighth-best among hitters with at least 900 plate appearances during that time span. At one point in 2024, that put him on a quest for a .400 batting average, before a rise in his launch angle contributed to what was a disappointing, .206 second-half batting average. Kwan's game lacks power, and his raw speed dipped noticeably last season, so he'll need to decide just what kind of hitter he wants to be. As an elite-contact, .300-hitting, 20-SB player with minimal power, he'll remain valuable in any fantasy format, particularly points-based scoring. Consider him in the early rounds in those leagues and slightly later in rotisserie formats.

name: Gunnar Henderson
season_outlook: Henderson followed up his unanimous 2023 Rookie of the Year season with a 2024 that saw him hit 26 home runs through the Orioles' first 80 games, second-most in the majors (Aaron Judge, 30), and finish fourth in AL MVP balloting. While Henderson cooled somewhat in the power department during the season's second half -- nine home runs and .174 ISO in his final 64 contests -- his cumulative numbers nevertheless cemented him as one of the game's premier shortstops, both for real life and fantasy. He's a centerpiece of one of the game's best up-and-coming offenses and a genuine, annual 35/20 threat. He is a building-block piece in both points-based and dynasty leagues.

name: Jackson Chourio
season_outlook: Chourio's rookie season is tough to appreciate until it's put into the proper context. He became only the 17th rookie in history to register a 20/20 season, with his .275 batting average ranking ninth amongst that group, and he finished 49th overall on our Player Rater and tied for 86th in fantasy points scored. Looking closer, Chourio began the season just 18 days past his 20th birthday, fresh off signing a record-setting contract for a player with no MLB experience, while also bearing a reputation for initial struggles when climbing competitive levels. He did stumble initially, with a .623 OPS through his first 67 games, but then he took off. Chourio's .309 batting average across his final 81 contests was ninth-best among qualifiers, and he scored the 11th-most fantasy points among hitters during that time span. The sky's the limit for this kid, who could very quickly establish himself as a perennial first-round fantasy pick in any format.

name: Jose Altuve
season_outlook: The Astros gave Altuve a vote of long-term confidence last February in the form of a five-year extension and he rewarded their continued faith with a 20-20 season, his first such season since 2017. Altuve earned his ninth All-Star selection with a .306 average and 14 homers in the first half before dipping to .277 and six, respectively, in the second half. The second baseman has always made the most of his talents and continues to take advantage of the Crawford Boxes in Houston, slugging more than 100 points higher at home versus on the road last season. Gone are the days of first-round value, but Altuve can still provide well-round production, with his greatest contributions at this stage coming in runs and batting average. Altuve, nearing his 35th birthday in May, has been mostly healthy in recent years outside of 2023 when he missed nearly half the season with thumb and oblique injuries.

name: Maikel Garcia
season_outlook: Garcia played in 157 games last year, but he holds the dubious distinction of his 69 wRC+ being the lowest among all qualified hitters. Fortunately, he swiped 37 bags, the seventh most in MLB. His game is putting the ball in play, mostly on the ground. His Hard-Hit rate and average exit velocity are above average, but not stout enough to supply much pop in power-suppressing Kauffman Stadium. Garcia is not a patient batter, so his time at or near the top of the order are likely over, especially with Jonathan India and a healthy Vinnie Pasquantino in tow. Even though Garcia's skills and defense are best suited for a utility role, he's slated to man the hot corner again in 2025. Even so, relying on Garcia for steals is a slippery slope, since someone else, such as Cavan Biggio, could cut into Garcia's playing time. Having dual second and third base eligibility sweetens Garcia's charm as a streamer in daily formats.

name: Nico Hoerner
season_outlook: One of baseball's best contact hitters, Hoerner has managed back-to-back top-80 fantasy seasons (in both roto and points-based formats) despite the fact that he hit just 16 home runs combined over those years. No, he's no power source, but his plate approach fuels a consistently solid batting average, his above-average speed and smarts on the bases make him a strong source of steals, and his status in the upper third of the Cubs lineup fuels a good number of plate appearances and runs scored. Hoerner's biggest knock entering 2025 is that he's coming off October flexor tendon surgery, which could threaten his Opening Day status. If he's looking good in March, however, he's one of the game's more underrated players, and well worth an early-round pick.

name: Jarren Duran
season_outlook: What a breakthrough Duran's 2024 campaign was! Few players have made as many all-around strides as he has over the past three years. He set personal bests in most every statistical category -- many of them by substantial margins -- culminating in his finishing 13th on our Player Rater and 18th overall in fantasy points scored. Most importantly, Duran, once a defensive liability, managed the eighth-best Statcast Fielding Run Value among outfielders, his strength in that department very much behind his MLB-leading 735 plate appearances. That amount of playing time will be tough to replicate, meaning some pull-back in his numbers is to be expected. Still, as a top-of-the-order Red Sox hitter, Duran should remain a top-50 fantasy performer regardless of format.

name: William Contreras
season_outlook: It's not often you'll see a catcher deliver the kind of breakthrough 2023 season that Contreras had and then following it up with an even more productive campaign. The No. 1 catcher from that year's Player Rater, and second-best in fantasy points, the Brewers backstop not only led his position in both scoring formats in 2024, but finished 28th in fantasy points and 44th on the Player Rater overall. Maintaining the contact and plate-discipline gains he exhibited two years ago was key to this transformation, and Contreras' jump into the 91st percentile in hard-hit rate last season reflects his status as one of the position's best power sources. He mashes left-handed pitchers -- FYI daily leaguers -- and should be the first catcher off the board in all fantasy formats.

name: Alex Bregman
season_outlook: Bregman's elite plate discipline makes him a valued points-league fantasy player. However, he was only 56th in scoring in 2024, after finishing top-30 in four of the previous six seasons. Maybe his middling contact-quality metrics have begun to catch up with him? A .276/.325/.532, 17-HR performance across his final 62 games offered encouragement that his 2022-24 baselines can be repeated, but the fact remains that he hasn't had a better-than-46th-percentile Statcast Barrel or better-than-51st-percentile hard hit rate since 2018. Where Bregman signs as a free agent will have a say in his fantasy utility -- players with his on-base skills fluctuate more in value based upon who hits behind them and how often their teams' lineups turn over. Until that's known, he's an early-round pick in points leagues and more of a borderline top-100 type in rotisserie.

name: Junior Caminero
season_outlook: A popular pick for AL Rookie of the Year honors entering last season, Caminero's ascent to Tampa Bay was instead delayed by a pair of IL trips due to quadriceps injuries while in Triple-A. He finally got his MLB chance in August, delivering what would have been better-than-70th-percentile Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates with an above-average contact rate that illustrates his massive offensive upside. Caminero should begin 2025 promised the Rays' everyday 3B role, as well as a heart-of-the-order lineup position. A significant step forward should be well within his reach. He's a potential top-10 positional fantasy option, regardless of format.

name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
season_outlook: Defense doesn't count in fantasy baseball scoring, but Crow-Armstrong's highlight reel glovework helps keep his bat in the lineup. He hits the ball with more authority than others that are reliant on steals for fantasy purposes, but he strikes out more and lacks patience. Crow-Armstrong also hits more fly balls than a typical speed merchant. A lot must come together, but Crow-Armstrong has the makings of a fantasy star, though that's not likely in 2025. He must first learn to make better swing decisions, so he can best blend his power and speed potential. For now, consider Crow-Armstrong a source of cheap steals, but be prepared to absorb a low batting average.

name: Luis Arraez
season_outlook: Batting average used to be the ultimate measure of a hitter, but times have changed. Arraez, the three-time reigning batting champion, is now often referred to dismissively as a one-trick pony by fans and fantasy players. That may seem harsh, but there is no getting around the fact that Arraez's batting averages have been empty. Real GMs have found themselves coming to terms with his limitations as a player, with Arraez having already been traded twice and also mentioned in the rumor mill this winter. He added a little bit of speed last season, but Arraez has reached double-digit homers only once, and a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Helping his case is eligibility at both first base and second base entering 2025.

name: Trea Turner
season_outlook: Turner was limited to 121 games last season as a left hamstring strain cost him a bit over six weeks in May and June. He continues to be productive on the wrong side of 30, though anyone so reliant on his legs takes on a little more risk with each season. Turner's sprint speed registered in the 96th percentile in 2024, so the league's smoothest slider still has wheels. Turner's quality of contact is around league average, so he needs speed to continue to be among the league leaders in infield hits. Last season, Turner stole 10 bases in 33 games before getting hurt, but then he swiped just four bags in the subsequent 63 contests after returning before adding five more over his final 25 games, with the lull in the middle was likely due to protecting his hamstring. Turner is no longer among the elite shortstops, but he heads up the next tier.

name: Brent Rooker
season_outlook: Rooker's arrival on the fantasy baseball scene has been quite unexpected. After changing teams three times during the course of 2022, he began 2023 as a platoon man only to burst forth with 30 homers. He followed it up with an even bigger breakthrough, finishing among the top eight in the majors with his 39 homers and a 16.6% Barrel rate in 2024. So where does Rooker, who signed a five-year, $60 million extension in January, go from here? The Athletics' move to Sacramento places them in a more hitter-friendly home environment for 2025, and the team's rekindled commitment to spending strengthened his prospects for a fantasy repeat. Even as a DH-only player initially, Rooker is well worth a mid-round pick.

name: George Springer
season_outlook: A prospect's growth isn't always linear and a veteran's decline isn't always gradual. Case in point: Springer. There is a chance Springer enjoys a renaissance season in 2025, but his quality of contact metrics are quickly heading in the wrong direction and they usually don't reverse at 35 years old. Springer's hard-hit rate and average exit velocity were career lows last season. In addition, his groundball rate has increased each of the last three seasons, sapping power. Once a top-of-the-order mainstay, Springer is now best suited for the lower half of the lineup. Solid plate skills keep Springer fantasy relevant, but there is arguably more downside than upside at this stage.

name: Josh Naylor
season_outlook: Naylor set career highs in games played, plate appearances, homers, runs and RBI last season. Volume was clearly a factor, but a career-high ISO was also a major contributor. Naylor needed the boost in power since he was unable to maintain the prior season's batted-ball fortune. The power spike could be fleeting for a number of reasons. Above all, Chase Field in Arizona, his new home venue, suppresses lefty power unlike his old digs in Cleveland which amplifies left-handed pop. A low strikeout rate and a projected spot in the middle of the Diamondbacks' order give Naylor a draftable floor, but plan on a modest power decline.

name: James Wood
season_outlook: A big, powerful prospect, albeit one with a good amount of swing-and-miss in his game, Wood should make a sizable leap in the home run category in 2025. After hitting 26 homers in 129 minor league games in 2023, then another 10 in 52 games for Triple-A Rochester to begin last season, he arrived in Washington to deliver what would have been 95th-percentile-or-better exit velocity and hard-hit rates. Wood will need to get more lift in his swing to realize his massive home run potential -- his ground-ball rate was 55% as a rookie -- but between that possibility and the above-average speed that has helped him average 18 steals across four professional seasons, he'll be plenty appealing as a breakthrough pick in rotisserie leagues as is. Consider him in the middle rounds.

name: Eugenio Suarez
season_outlook: Suarez made the most of his change of scenery and had his best season at the plate since 2019. That 2019 season will not be replicated, but for Suarez to hit 30 homers and drive in 100-plus in a neutral offensive environment with baseballs that were not traveling as far last year says something. Suarez continues to be a fastball destroyer and he remains quite capable of punishing mistakes. The third baseman still has a good amount of swing and miss in his game, which can lead to some serious peaks and valleys. To that point, he had just 10 homers and a .216/.302/.366 line at the All Star break last season. Suarez hitting 20 homers with a .307/.341/.602 line in the second half won some leagues and quieted the doubters who thought 2023 was the start of an acceleration into the aging curve.

name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
season_outlook: In 2024, many things went just right for Chisholm, a power/speed rotisserie gem for fantasy managers (albeit one with a penchant for injuries). He boosted his contact rate, improving his month-over-month consistency at the plate, played a career-best 147 games, and flourished following a midseason trade to the Yankees, batting .275/.325/.500 with 11 homers and 18 steals in 46 regular-season games in pinstripes. What's more, Chisholm adapted nicely to his new role at third base in New York, and his projected status as their second baseman to begin 2025 might quickly make him eligible at three positions. He might always be at risk of missing time with future ailments, but he's in a great spot for above-average power and elite speed, a combination that gives him top-50 overall upside in rotisserie formats. Bear in mind, however, that Chisholm's value in points-based and sabermetric scoring is a couple of tiers below that.

name: Salvador Perez
season_outlook: Whereas most catchers wear down rather quickly due the rigors of the position, Perez is still running strong at nearly 35 years old. He exceeded 100 RBI last season for the second time in his career and surged past 20 homers once again en route to his fifth Silver Slugger Award. Perez is the active leader in games played at catcher and 58th on the all-time list. The Royals have made a concerted effort to limit Perez's time behind the plate in recent years, giving him more time at first base and DH, which makes all the sense in the world given the mileage on Perez's knees and with Freddy Fermin proving plenty capable of helping with the workload. Perez is firmly in the old-and-boring category, but his track record of power production from the catcher spot should keep his services in high demand in fantasy baseball.

name: Christian Yelich
season_outlook: Yelich's troublesome back finally forced him under the knife in August, ending his season. Specifically, the procedure was a microdiscectomy, a spinal surgery to remove part or all of a bulging or herniated disc. While Yelich was still not cleared to swing a bat as of mid-December, the team is expecting him to be ready early on in spring training. The outfielder produced at a high level in between IL stints last season, slashing .315/.406/.504 with 11 homers and 21 steals in just 73 games. The back now being surgically repaired offers hope that Yelich could stay on the field and return to something close to his previous levels of production, though it would be unwise to expect him to return an MVP level for the Brewers at 33 years old.

name: Seiya Suzuki
season_outlook: Suzuki's name has been mentioned in trade rumors, but the Cubs' asking price is high and justifiably so given he has been well above league average at the plate in each of his three seasons in the majors. Suzuki spent time on the injured list again last season and saw his strikeout rate increase, but he kept his batting average over .280 and reached 20 homers for the second straight year. Taking advantage of the bigger bases and new rules limiting pickoff attempts, Suzuki went from six steals in 2023 to 16 last season. The reason the Cubs are willing to listen at all is his defense in the outfield, which was so shaky that the team decided to move him to designated hitter down the stretch. However, Suzuki has said that he does not want to be a full-time DH, which leaves open questions about his future. No matter where he ends up, Suzuki will be in the lineup nearly every day in 2025 since his bat is too good to keep on the bench.

name: Vinnie Pasquantino
season_outlook: The ?Pasquatch? is an underrated hitter, especially for points-based scoring. Coming off a 2023 that saw him miss more than three months due to shoulder surgery, Pasquantino joined Yandy Diaz as the only qualified hitters in baseball with at least a 45% hard-hit but no greater than a 15% whiff rate on swings, even if his rotisserie numbers weren't anything special. Unfortunately, further bad luck in the injury department still holds him back as he missed September thanks to a broken thumb. With greater luck in 2025, he has the skills and the prime-age status to become a top-five points based (and top-10 rotisserie) first baseman. Consider taking Pasquantino in the early rounds in points leagues.

name: Riley Greene
season_outlook: Greene, the No. 5 overall pick of the 2019 amateur draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2022 rookie season, has made incremental gains across his three MLB campaigns to date. Unfortunately, those have also included extensive -- though generally unlucky -- absences, from the fractured right foot that delayed his arrival in Detroit in 2022, to the fractured left fibula that cost him five weeks of 2023, the Tommy John surgery that prematurely ended his 2023 in early September and the hamstring strain that cost him three weeks last summer. When healthy, Greene's contact-quality metrics are stellar, akin to those you'd expect from an All-Star. With some better fortune in the injury department, he could be ready to join the top-50 players in fantasy baseball in 2025.

name: Will Smith
season_outlook: Smith's wRC+ declined for the fourth straight season, but his 111 mark was still one of the top efforts from a catcher, especially one with the sixth most plate appearances at the position. With Shohei Ohtani joining the Dodgers, Smith only served as the DH three times. However, there is evidence that his drop in production wasn't necessarily due to the extra games behind the plate. April was by far Smith's best month with a .397 wOBA, then the final five months fell between .279 and .332, with September being his second-best month. Since 2021, only Salvador Perez has had more plate appearances as a backstop and just J.T. Realmuto has caught more innings than Smith, so a gentle drop in exit velocity and Hard-Hit rate is understandable. Even so, Smith's quality and quantity of contact remain solid for the position, keeping Smith among the first backstops off the board.

name: Shea Langeliers
season_outlook: A three-homer game during the second full week of the season set the tone for Langeliers' 2024 campaign, as he finished second on the team to Brent Rooker in both home runs and RBI with 29 and 80, respectively. Langeliers cut a couple points off his strikeout rate which helped lift his batting average from .205 to a slightly more palatable .224. Slugging will have to carry Langeliers' offensive game since he has a strikeout rate of nearly 30 percent for his career, and the Athletics' move to a Pacific Coast League park in West Sacramento should help in that regard in 2025. Even with the low average and limited time at DH to boost his stats, Langeliers will likely be drafted as a top-10 catcher in many leagues.

name: CJ Abrams
season_outlook: Abrams appeared in only 138 games last season, but half of the missed time occurred in September when he missed out on the last eight games of the season after being demoted to Triple-A for staying out all night prior to a day game. Despite a second-half swoon, Abrams improved his hard-hit rate overall and experienced an uptick in power. The added production helped mitigate a drop in steals. In 2023, Abrams swiped 47 bags in 51 tries for an outstanding 92 percent success rate. Last season, he was just 31-for-43 (72 percent). Still just 24 years old, Abrams is expected to learn from last season's disciplinary action and continue maturing as a person and player. The arrows are pointing upward, especially if he can cut down on last season's caught stealing number.

name: Gleyber Torres
season_outlook: While many might regard Torres' career thus far as a disappointment, he has nevertheless carved out a plenty productive role for himself. Over his seven MLB seasons, his 138 home runs rank third-most among second basemen and he's one of only four at the position with at least 100 homers and 50 steals. Torres did benefit from the hitter-friendly home environment of Yankee Stadium, as well as the often potent Yankees lineup, so some regression is to be expected now that he's a member of the Tigers. Still, Torres seems to have settled in as an annual 25-HR, 10-SB, .265-hitting type with top-10 positional fantasy value. Plus, he did finish an underwhelming 2024 on a high note (.297/.369/.453, 7 HR over his final 45 games, playoffs included). Expect similar value from him in 2025.

name: Brice Turang
season_outlook: Turang is a throwback to 1980s baseball in that he makes the most of his speed. He is a pesky hitter who will work counts, fight off pitches and then put one into play, often to the opposite field, before turning on the burners. Turang plays within himself, realizing that double-digit homers are likely out of the picture most seasons, though his profile leaves him very much at the mercy of BABIP fortunes. Turang strikes out approximately once every five at bats, yet only Jake Cronenworth has a lower batting average over the past two seasons for all players with similar strikeout rates or better. The difference with most of the other names on the list is they make more consistent hard contact while Turang's contact metrics are all bottom 20th percentile. This profile fits at the bottom third of the lineup, leaving him plenty of chances to run but also making it difficult to reach even 80 runs scored.

name: Ian Happ
season_outlook: Happ tied a career high with 25 home runs in 2024 and also set career bests in runs (89) and RBI (86), while his .782 OPS remained in line with his marks from the previous two seasons. The veteran outfielder also recorded double-digit steals (13) for the second consecutive campaign, which he didn't accomplish in his first six big-league seasons. He continues to showcase his patience and finished tied-fifth in MLB with 80 walks, and he has a double-digit walk rate in four of the past five years. Happ has also won three straight Gold Gloves in left field for the Cubs, which helps him stick in the lineup through any slumps. He's played in nearly 96 percent of Chicago's games over the past five years and has provided a consistently above-average bat throughout his career, so Happ should be a reliable target for fantasy managers in 2025.

name: Teoscar Hernandez
season_outlook: One of baseball's most consistent power sources, but also one of its most free-swinging hitters, Hernandez has hit 25-plus homers in each of the last five full MLB seasons and 32-plus in two of his last four. By returning to the Dodgers this winter, he chose to remain in one of the game's better home run environments, as well as one of its most potent lineups. Hernandez should again deliver value akin to his 2024, which had him a top-25 rotisserie and top-75 overall points league performer.

name: Jackson Merrill
season_outlook: In almost any other year, Merrill's 2024 breakthrough would have secured him a Rookie of the Year Award. He became only the fifth rookie in history with at least a .290 batting average, 20 HR, 90 RBI and 15  SB. The previous four all took home top rookie honors (Orlando Cepeda 1958, Nomar Garciaparra 1997, Carlos Beltran 1999, Ryan Braun 2007). Tuck that away if Merrill's value in your draft remotely softens, especially in light of his late-season skills improvement, as he hit .314/.349/.596 with 7% more fly balls after the All-Star break than before it. He no longer carries shortstop eligibility, but that doesn't make him any less attractive of an outfield pick in the early rounds. In keeper leagues, Merrill is a building block.

name: Yordan Alvarez
season_outlook: Few players hit the baseball with greater authority than Alvarez. Across six MLB seasons, his 53.2% Statcast hard-hit rate is third-best (minimum 1,000 plate appearances), his 93.5 mph average exit velocity is sixth-best and his 17.1% Barrel rate is seventh-best. He's one of only five players with 30-plus homers in each of the past four seasons and, among those five, his .296 batting average trails only Aaron Judge's .300. Alvarez's main differentiators from the game's elite are his injury history -- he has made seven trips to the IL  -- and a lack of hardware, statistical records or a big free-agent contract. That might, however, make him a relative discount among players who deserve selection during the first two rounds.

name: Yandy Diaz
season_outlook: After teasing a late-career power surge in 2023, Diaz reverted to his previous power levels last season. Overall, Diaz continues to sport elite quality of contact metrics, but since he hits grounders more than half of the time, he is unable to take full advantage. Not only did Diaz's power drop, but his batting average with runners in scoring position fell 90 points, limiting his RBI. After carrying a double-digit walk rate over the previous five seasons, Diaz's patience waned last season, leaving him with the second-lowest OBP of his career. Diaz is best suited for points leagues, where his high doubles total can help mitigate fewer homers. Look for a rebound, but 2023 will likely go down as Diaz's career year.

name: Randy Arozarena
season_outlook: Arozarena's stock has fallen in the past calendar year. He got off to a brutal start to 2024 with a .461 OPS through the end of April and the Rays later traded him to the Mariners for a pair of prospects and a player to be named later, in line with their usual modus operandi. The outfielder first broke out in the 2020 playoffs when he hit 10 homers, most in postseason history, and in the years since he's turned in four consecutive 20-20 seasons. However, T-Mobile Park in Seattle was the worst in baseball for offense last season by MLB's own park factors, and the lineup around him is underwhelming. Worst of all for his long-term outlook, Arozarena's defense has been dismal in recent years, wiping out a lot of his value to real-world teams. Eventually, that will cost him playing time and the volume will no longer be there to prop him up.

name: Byron Buxton
season_outlook: Buxton exclusively worked at designated hitter throughout 2023 in an attempt to keep him healthy, but he played in just 85 contests before returning to center field for the Twins last season. His return to the outfield was overall a success as his 102 games played represented his largest workload since 2017, but he still battled injuries and has reached 400 plate appearances in a season just once in his big-league career. Buxton took a major step backward at the plate in 2023, but he rebounded last year with 18 home runs and a .279/.335/.524 slash line, with the resurgence being supported by a 48.1 percent hard-hit rate. The 31-year-old has played in just over 57 percent of Minnesota's games across the past three seasons, so 90-100 games is a reasonable estimate for him in 2025. Fantasy managers will obviously be hoping for more than that, especially coming off a clean offseason, but expectations should still be tempered given his lengthy injury history.

name: Corey Seager
season_outlook: Injuries once again hampered Seager, who has now spent time on the IL in five of his past seven seasons, resulting in a combined 333 regular-season games missed over that stretch. A hip issue cut his 2024 short in early September, and hernia surgeries bookended his season (one in January, one in September). Nevertheless, Seager remained healthy enough to hit 30-plus homers for the third consecutive season and, at the time he got hurt, he had the sixth-most fantasy points among shortstops and 25th-most of all hitters. His underlying metrics, too, were as good as they have been at any point during the past five seasons, signaling that he's still every bit the early-round pick.

name: Brandon Nimmo
season_outlook: Once an on-base machine, Nimmo has seen his OBP fall from over .400 during his peak years to just .327 last season. His batting average fell 50 points to .224, ranking in the bottom 12 among qualified hitters, while his slugging dipped below .400. The outfielder still fell just one homer shy of his career high of 24 established the year prior, and he set a new career high with 15 steals in as many attempts. It came to light in October that Nimmo had been playing through plantar fasciitis since May, which explains some of the issues, though if it was such a hindrance, it doesn't make much sense that he was running more than ever. Regardless, Nimmo is now something of a wild card entering his age-32 season given the sudden decline in rate stats. The Mets signed him to an eight-year extension prior to the 2023 season and will be hoping for a bounce-back campaign.

name: Bo Bichette
season_outlook: Once a first-round stalwart, Bichette is coming off a terrible season ravaged by injuries. A .599 OPS after a three-year mark of .815 is especially troublesome, though a 43.5 percent hard-hit rate last season offers hope, as does a clean bill of health after finger surgery. At least doubling last season's 4.4 percent barrel rate is key, and plausible if healthy. Bichette's steals have fallen since he swiped 25 in 26 tries in 2021, but he did notch five bags in what amounts to half a season last year, so a return to double-digit pilfers is in play. By his own account, Bichette tried to be more selective and has vowed to return to a more free-swinging approach. The cost to learn if Bichette re-enters the circle of trust is nominal compared to the reward.

name: Mike Trout
season_outlook: From a pure baseball perspective, it's a shame that Trout's career has trended downwards from one-time contender for "best player in baseball history" to merely a certain first-ballot Hall of Famer. Injuries have been a persistent problem for him across the last eight seasons, but especially the past four, during which he has missed more Angels games while on the IL (360) than he has played (266). Those ailments, and probably also the aging curve (he's now 33) have diminished his once-blazing speed as well as begun to erode his top-shelf contact quality. Even accounting for all that, Trout is still one of the game's most stellar talents. This guy, after all, hit 10 homers across his first 25 games of 2024. His power and patience remain his most marketable fantasy skills, ideal for points-based and sabermetric scoring, but Trout is more of a mid- than early-round pick these days with the many questions surrounding his durability.

name: Ozzie Albies
season_outlook: Albies is a three-time All-Star and two-time Silver Slugger, but injuries have kept him under 100 games played in two of the past three seasons. First, a fractured right toe put him on the shelf last year before a fractured left wrist cost him most of the summer. There was some uncertainty as to whether he would return last season, but Albies made it back for nine games at the very end of the campaign. In addition to the injuries, there have been chirps that Albies could or perhaps should give up switch hitting given his career splits as a left-handed hitter against right-handed pitching (.247/.309/.434). Despite the flaws in his profile, Albies is arguably still right up there among the top second basemen on the board, maybe behind only Ketel Marte. As he enters his age-28 season, Albies will be attempting to turn the page on his recent health woes and return to 30-10 production for Atlanta.

name: Taylor Ward
season_outlook: Ward established new career highs in plate appearances (663), hits (144) and home runs (25) last season, leading the Angels in all three categories. He still has not been able to replicate the full extent of his success from 2022 when he slashed .281/.360/.473 over 564 plate appearances, but Ward's 2024 season represented a bright spot for the organization as well as an impressive personal rebound. Remember, his 2023 campaign was cut short when he suffered multiple facial fractures on a hit-by-pitch and there are often mental hurdles that accompany such an injury. Ward's strikeout rate ticked up to close to 25 percent last season, but he was still an above-average offensive contributor, and as he enters his age-31 season, he appears set to continue anchoring the heart of the order for Anaheim.

name: Matt Chapman
season_outlook: Chapman didn't sign until March 1 last year, but he didn't let the late start affect him as he went on to achieve his best offensive season this decade. The third baseman popped 27 homers and ranked seventh in the National League in runs scored with 98. He added a speed element last season, swiping 15 bags in 17 attempts, which was rather surprising considering he stole 11 bases in his first seven MLB seasons combined. That said, Chapman is no statue and it's reasonable to think he could reach double-digit steals once again in 2025 considering the recent rule changes facilitating the running game and stolen bases in particular. The rest of Chapman's game looks fairly stable, including playing time given his excellent defense at the hot corner. Expect a relatively low average but useful counting stats in his age-32 season.

name: Brendan Donovan
season_outlook: Contact is the name of the game with Donovan, who sits with a 13.7 percent strikeout rate and an even .280 average through 1,491 career plate appearances. His bat is lacking in terms of thump, however, ranking in the bottom half of the league in average exit velocity and hard-hit rate last season. Donovan logged 652 plate appearances in 2024, second on the team to Paul Goldschmidt, but he managed just 14 homers and five steals, providing fantasy managers with little category juice. He's more than a slap hitter, but Donovan's value is heavily dependent on volume, more so than other hitters in his range. Similar volume is projected in 2025, and eligibility at second base and outfield gives Donovan unique and valuable flexibility.

name: Yainer Diaz
season_outlook: William Contreras finished last season on an island alone as the No. 1 fantasy catcher, but Diaz was right there in that second tier of earners just behind Cal Raleigh and Salvador Perez, at least in traditional leagues scoring batting average. Diaz finished fifth at the position in plate appearances with 619 and ranked eighth among all qualified hitters with a .299 average. It was an impressive showing after the Astros turned over the reins behind the plate, even if Diaz wasn't able to replicate the kind of power he showed as a rookie in 2023. In fact, Diaz hit seven fewer homers in 44 additional games. Nonetheless, Diaz established himself further and will be treated as a top catching option behind the younger Contreras entering 2025. Those in OBP leagues will likely want to bump Diaz down to account for a career walk rate of just 3.6 percent.

name: Jung Hoo Lee
season_outlook: Lee suffered a season-ending shoulder injury in May when he crashed into the outfield fence at Oracle Park, necessitating surgery. The expectation is that Lee will be a full go for the start of spring training in 2025 as he enters Year 2 of a six-year contract with the Giants following a storied career with the Kiwoom Heroes of the Korea Baseball Organization. At age 25, Lee debuted in the majors with a .289 batting average across his first 20 games before dipping to .226 across his subsequent 17 games. It was a rather tiny sample in the end, but the contact that he was known for in the KBO translated, with Lee striking out just 13 times across 158 plate appearances. The big question is whether Lee can tap into enough power to be worthwhile in mixed leagues, but that may be tough in San Francisco. It's also possible that Lee could lose out on some at-bats against left-handed pitching.

name: Michael Harris II
season_outlook: Harris had a whirlwind season in 2024, going from a .304 batting average in the first month to a .200 average in May to landing on the injured list in June. His injury was classified as a Grade 2 strain of his left hamstring and the outfielder ended up shifting to the 60-day IL before returning in August. Harris ultimately bookended his campaign with an impressive month of September in which he slashed .316/.344/.579 with eight homers. He was regularly batting leadoff down the stretch and could very well remain there to begin 2025 with Ronald Acuna expected to miss at least the first month while recovering from knee surgery. A low walk rate threatens to relegate Harris back to the lower third eventually, but if he stays on the field he could finally reach 20-20 with Atlanta after falling just short in 2022 and 2023.

name: Adley Rutschman
season_outlook: Rutschman's smooth, year-over-year ascent to the top of the fantasy catcher rankings hit a roadblock last June. Through his first 77 games, he was batting .300/.351/.480 with 15 home runs and was the top-scoring fantasy catcher. After being struck on the hand with a foul tip, however, he hit just .189/.279/.280 with four homers over his final 71 games. Given the injury, it's rational to forgive Rutschman for the sluggish finish. Even though his spring training bears closer watching than usual, he's a prime-age 27 after being the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 amateur draft. He has drawn rave reviews from scouts for years, so it's easy to make the case that Rutschman remains a fantasy building block and a sound early-round pick regardless of format.

name: Jacob Wilson
season_outlook: One of the game's best hit-tool prospects, Wilson posted a .412 batting average and 97% contact rate in his final college season at Grand Canyon, .333/89% numbers in his 26-game pro debut in 2023, and .433/.93% numbers as a minor leaguer in 2024. That earned him a mid-July promotion to the Athletics, where he unfortunately suffered a hamstring injury in his MLB debut that cost him the next five weeks. Wilson returned to record similarly strong contact metrics as the team's starting shortstop down the stretch, and he figures to serve in the same role to begin 2025. He's lacking in much else at this stage of his career, but this is the kind of high-floor player mixed-leaguers should want from their middle infield spot.

name: Wyatt Langford
season_outlook: A popular preseason pick for 2024 AL Rookie of the Year honors, Langford instead struggled mightily in his first taste of the majors, batting just .227/.287/.300 with only seven extra-base hits across his first 40 games. As many a rookie has done before, however, he picked up the pace from there, culminating in June AL Rookie of the Month and September AL Player and Rookie of the Month honors. For the season as a whole, Langford's metrics were well above-average across the board, giving hope that the superstardom predicted for him at this point one year ago remains his future track. He should not be allowed to linger too deep into the middle rounds of any draft.

name: Jeremy Pena
season_outlook: Pena now has three full major-league seasons under his belt. He has hit 20 homers in a season and he has also stolen 20 bases in a season, but the shortstop has been unable to accomplish both feats in the same campaign. Pena has the pull tendencies one would like to see from someone playing in Houston and hitting from the right side, but his high groundball rate limits his home-run power. Pena has improved his strikeout rate each season he has been in the majors, but he has not shown any willingness to accepts walks. Pena has also stolen double-digit bases each season, but his success rate has been below league average since the rule adjustments two seasons ago. His impatience puts him in the bottom half of the lineup which limits his overall upside, and it's a shame because Pena's numbers could be much better if he were setting the table ahead of the thunder in the lineup.

name: Alec Bohm
season_outlook: Bohm's name has been bandied about in trade rumors this winter ahead of his second year of arbitration eligibility. The Phillies are said to be eyeing a roster shakeup of sorts, but so far no team has met Philadelphia's asking price for the third baseman. Bohm had some tough times early in his big-league career, but he's been on the upswing since his infamous "I hate this place" incident in 2022, making his first All-Star team this past season. He hit five fewer homers than he did in 2023, totaling just 15 despite similar batted-ball numbers, following league-wide trends. Bohm has grounded into 41 double plays over the past two seasons which shows his below-average running ability, but at this point he's established as a dependable source of batting average and run production.

name: Bryson Stott
season_outlook: Stott now has three big-league seasons under his belt. He has the skills and athleticism to hit higher in the lineup for another team, but it will be for him to crack the top third of the Philadelphia order while Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Bryce Harper are healthy. If stuck in the nine hole, his RBI chances will remain limited. Stott is one of just three second basemen to register double-digit homers and steals in each of the past three seasons, joining only Jose Altuve and Mookie Betts. Stott contributes across the board and some BABIP regression would help him recover some of the 35 points in batting average he lost from 2023 to 2024.

name: Willy Adames
season_outlook: Adames parlayed what was a career year on many fronts into a seven-year, $182 million contract with the Giants -- one of the offseason's earliest signings. He'll now play in a more challenging hitting environment than during his three and a half years in Milwaukee. Playing in the Brewers' HR-friendly home ballpark, Adames managed personal bests with his 32 home runs, 112 RBI, 93 runs scored, 153 hits, 33 doubles, 21 stolen bases, 74 walks and 282 total bases last season, while also pacing all major leaguers with 224 plate appearances and 93 RBI with runners in scoring position. The park switch assures some regression in the power departments, as does the good fortune in the RBI column. Nevertheless, Adames is a prime-age hitter who should put forth top-10 positional numbers in all fantasy formats.

name: Willson Contreras
season_outlook: The Cardinals announced in November that Contreras will be a full-time first baseman and designated hitter moving forward. It brings to an end a rather strange saga in which the team soured on his catching abilities shortly after signing him, moving him out from behind the plate for a stretch previously in 2023. Contreras fractured his forearm on a catcher's interference in May of last year when he was struck by a J.D. Martinez swing, and he broke a finger on a HBP later in the season. He still managed 15 home runs in just 84 games, and Contreras has been above league average at the plate in every single season of his career. Now 34 and overshadowed by his younger brother, Contreras will potentially get lost in the shuffle at first base when he loses catcher eligibility in 2026, but he should still be treated as a premium option at the catcher position for 2025.

name: Nolan Arenado
season_outlook: After an offseason flooded with trade rumors, Arenado returns to St. Louis for a fifth season. His performance has taken a step backwards in both of the last two campaigns, coinciding with the typical downward aging curve a player set to turn 34 years old in April might follow. Back and forearm injuries in those seasons might have played a part, but Arenado has never seen such poor contact-quality metrics as he did in 2024. He'll need to reverse those to remain a top-10 capable fantasy third baseman, and it's not unheard of that a player of his caliber can squeeze out one more productive year at this stage of his career. It's still wiser to regard Arenado a mid-round, mid-range pick unless he looks great during the exhibition season.

name: Oneil Cruz
season_outlook: Cruz is making good on the hype and there is still room for growth as he enters his age-26 season. He cracked 21 homers and swiped 22 bags in 23 attempts last year, showcasing his loud tools and athleticism. There were some lingering issues with his left ankle after he missed nearly all of 2023 with a fracture, but the Pirates have said that they do not expect the ankle to be a long-term concern. The team moved him from shortstop to center field in late August, which seemed rather sudden at the time although it was not entirely unexpected given Cruz was always an anomaly as a 6-foot-7 shortstop. A strikeout rate over 30 percent for his career gives him some downside in batting average, but optimists can reasonably dream on another level of upside in home runs and stolen bases in 2025.

name: Xander Bogaerts
season_outlook: Bogaerts started slowly last season, batting .219/.265/.316 over 47 games, perhaps due to learning a new position after an unexpected shift from shortstop to second base. He then suffered a nasty shoulder injury in May, costing him almost two months. After returning, Bogaerts settled in and hit .299/.338/.432 the rest of the way, in line with his 2023 production. His power never developed as hoped and now it's on the decline with three straight seasons of a falling barrel rate. However, Bogaerts has taken advantage of the rules aiding stolen bases, swiping 32 bases in 37 attempts over the past two years. His bat-to-ball skills are still solid, propping up his floor, but there isn't much upside in power or speed. Dual eligibility adds to Bogaerts' appeal, especially in daily leagues.

name: Jurickson Profar
season_outlook: Coming off a miserable 2023, Profar rebounded with a career-best campaign in 2024, particularly in terms of his underlying plate discipline, contact quality and power metrics. Having a full spring training probably helped (he signed late in 2023), so it's a good thing that he found his 2025 team by mid-January. Also helpful was an adjustment to his batting stance, as a heightened leg kick helped him drive the ball better. Now with the Braves, Profar should benefit from hitting high in the order for one of the game's most potent lineups. If he can snag a top-two lineup position, he'd be in good shape to approach or repeat his 2024, so monitor his role closely. Even as a lower-in-the-order hitter, however, he'd be a worthwhile third or fourth fantasy outfielder.

name: Marcus Semien
season_outlook: After leading the majors in plate appearances for three consecutive years, Semien finished fourth last season with 718. His numbers were down across the board, though he still cracked 23 homers and reached triple digits in runs scored as the Rangers' primary leadoff hitter. Manager Bruce Bochy hinted in December that Semien, now 34, could get more days off in 2025 and beyond, and also said that he has floated the idea of moving Semien around the batting order. Semien has been barely above a .300 OBP in two of the past three years, so the move would be justified, but that combination of more days off and a lower spot in the order could wreak havoc on the second baseman's counting stats. His plate skills are holding steady and he can still run a bit, but Semien is trending in the wrong direction and the track record carries a bit less weight at this stage.

name: Isaac Paredes
season_outlook: Paredes was traded twice in the final sixth months of 2024, first to the Cubs and later to the Astros in the Kyle Tucker deal. The power dipped after his move from Tampa Bay to the North Side, but his new home in Houston looks like a great fit for Paredes' pull-heavy approach from the right side. Indeed the Crawford Boxes could help Paredes return to the 30-homer plateau, but a career .245 BABIP saddles him with a low batting average and speaks to his limited running ability. His batted-ball profile is not what one might expect, though Paredes is a unique player and the rules don't always apply to a hitter with his spray chart. The third baseman carries bonus first-base eligibility in leagues with a 15-game minimum.

name: Lawrence Butler
season_outlook: Butler used up his rookie eligibility in 2023 and had a .582 OPS in 42 games, but he was electric during his first full MLB campaign last year with 22 homers, 18 steals and a .262/.317/.490 slash line in 125 contests. He still endured some ups and downs, however, as he was demoted to Triple-A in May after posting a .555 OPS through 121 plate appearances. Butler rejoined the Athletics in mid-June and was one of the best hitters in baseball the rest of the way, and he clubbed 20 home runs in his final 84 games. The underlying numbers back up the production, so there shouldn't be any major worries about regression in 2025. Butler clearly has the potential to deliver a 20-20 campaign, and the move from The Coliseum in Oakland to the more hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park in Sacramento should help him build on the breakout season.

name: Austin Riley
season_outlook: Riley entered 2024 as one of the most consistent hitters in baseball with three straight 30-homer, 90-RBI seasons and an .878 OPS during that span, but he underwhelmed last year with a .256/.322/.461 slash line and 19 home runs through 110 games before a fractured hand ended his campaign in mid-August. Despite the drop in production, the veteran third baseman was still making consistent hard contact, which bodes well for a rebound in 2025. He should have a fairly typical offseason given the timing of the injury, so there's no real question on his status heading into spring training. Riley's .783 OPS in a down season illustrates his high floor, and there's a strong likelihood he bounces back to his All-Star form in 2025 given his track record and the fact he'll turn just 28 years old in April.

name: Marcell Ozuna
season_outlook: Ozuna has been on an amazing two-year run since nearly playing his way out of Atlanta with consecutive terrible seasons in 2021 and 2022. He served exclusively as a designated hitter and in fact started all 162 games at DH last season, returning to elite-level run production once again after it once looked as if 2017 was going to be his peak. Ozuna has driven in 100 runs in each of the past two seasons, and it was all the more impressive in 2024 considering the amount of injuries to the Atlanta lineup over the course of the season. The counting stats seem ultra stable, though his batting average has ranged from .213 to .338 over the past five seasons despite relatively stable walk and strikeout rates, which is a reminder of how is still left up to the randomness of the machinations of baseball. Ozuna may never score 100 runs, but there is little reason to suspect he cannot continue to this current run of success.

name: Nick Castellanos
season_outlook: Castellanos appeared in all 162 regular-season games last season before going 7-for-17 with a home run in the NLDS. By all accounts, he is well liked in the clubhouse, but despite all that, the Phillies have made it known that Castellanos is available via trade. So far, no move has gone down, but it is clear how the organization sees Castellanos at this stage -- not a great fit on a contending roster. The issue is his porous and only deteriorating defense in right field, which largely negates the value provided by his bat. As he enters his age-33 season, Castellanos is at risk of losing playing time, even if he stays in Philadelphia, give that he has not been a significant net positive in real life in any of the past three seasons. His 2025 fantasy value will depend entirely on whether or not he can maintain similar volume throughout the campaign.

name: Alejandro Kirk
season_outlook: Kirk spent four months in a timeshare before becoming the primary receiver in Toronto after Danny Jansen was dealt at the trade deadline. Kirk should remain the main man behind the plate as Blue Jays don't have any catching prospects in the pipeline and there are just journeyman backups to compete with the incumbent. Kirk's greatest asset is batting average, fueled by a near-elite strikeout rate. His hard-hit rate increased to 54th percentile last season, but as one of the slowest runners in the league, his BABIP is below average. Kirk is a two-trick pony, contributing in average and RBI, with the latter contingent on regular playing time and help from his teammates.

name: Tommy Edman
season_outlook: Edman spent the first four months of the 2024 campaign on the injured list as he recovered from offseason wrist surgery and didn't see game action until after being traded from the Cardinals to the Dodgers at the deadline. The utility man played in 37 games during the regular season and had a .237/.294/.417 slash line with six homers and six steals, but he got on track during the playoffs with an .862 OPS in 67 plate appearances. Edman then inked a five-year extension with Los Angeles early in the offseason and he is expected to serve as the club's primary center fielder in 2025, though he'll likely still see some time at other positions. He's spent most of his career playing second base and shortstop, but he may be limited to outfield eligibility to begin the season since he made just one appearance at second base and 18 at shortstop last year. Edman averaged 12 home runs, 30 steals, 85 runs and 53 RBI across the three seasons prior to 2024, and that type of production is likely a best-case scenario in his age-30 campaign.

name: Carlos Correa
season_outlook: Correa was an elite producer in 2024 with a .310/.388/.517 slash line, but the catch is he was limited to just 86 games due to plantar fasciitis in his right foot. He dealt with the same injury in his other foot in 2023, though he still played in 135 games while laboring to a .711 OPS. Correa returned to action for the final weeks of the 2024 regular season and raked despite still being clearly hobbled, but he's expected to begin spring training in good health. Now entering his age-30 campaign, the injury questions will only intensify for Correa, who has played 150 games in a season just once in his big-league career. That being said, he played in at least 130 contests the previous three seasons, with the extended absence last year being his first lengthy stay on the IL since 2019. Correa will likely be a major fantasy asset if he can stay healthy, but that's a significant "if" for the shortstop at this stage of his career.

name: Bryan Reynolds
season_outlook: Reynolds is a textbook Professional Hitter coming off four straight 20-homer seasons and back-to-back 20-10 campaigns. His batting average has not fallen below .260 in a full season and Reynolds has been an All-Star in two of the past four years since his fluke down year in 2020. While his defense in the outfield corners has fallen off a cliff, the Pirates have not seemed to mind nor have they indicated a positional change could be in the cards. Reynolds signed an eight-year contract extension in 2023 and will return to anchor the heart of the Pittsburgh order after batting exclusively out of the two hole last season -- typically where teams put their best hitter. Entering his age-30 season, Reynolds provides a stable floor in terms of skills and playing time.

name: Dansby Swanson
season_outlook: Swanson's 2024 was a lot like his 2023 in many ways. His rate stats were nearly identical, but 40 fewer plate appearances and a lower spot in the lineup affected his RBI total. Swanson was clearly battling some issues health-wise since he immediately had core muscle surgery once the season ended in order to be fully ready in time for spring training. By and large, Swanson continues to stay on the field and produce in all the counting categories, but 2022 may go down as his peak unless the prevailing winds in Wrigley happen to blow out more than they blow in. The numbers around his plate discipline are rather stable if slightly unspectacular. His strikeouts make it tough to envision him hitting over .270 again unless he is blessed with good batted-ball fortune.

name: Jordan Westburg
season_outlook: Westburg earned an All-Star selection in his age-25 season and showed that he should not get lost in the shuffle among the rest of the Orioles' talented young core. His season was interrupted by a fractured right hand, the result of a hit-by-pitch, which cost him most of the final two months. Before going down, Westburg posted an .815 OPS, 18 homers and six steals in 101 games. After serving as the Opening Day designated hitter, Westburg moved around the infield, securing eligibility at second base and third base again entering 2025. Baltimore announced in November that it will be modifying the left-field wall at Camden Yards, moving it in to find a "happier medium," per GM Mike Elias, after the club pushed the wall back prior to 2022. That bodes well for the right-handed-hitting Westburg, who projects to remain a lineup regular.

name: Anthony Santander
