season_outlook: Don't regard Santander's career-best, 44-HR explosion as a sign of his growing power, because his underlying metrics were almost spot-on to his 2022-23 rates, with Statcast's expected home runs having him pegged for only slightly more than he hit in either of those two years (36.6, versus 33.3 in 2022 and 2023). Santander's appeal in fantasy leagues is his consistency, as he has hit .244 while averaging 95 RBI, 83 runs scored and 153 games played across the past three seasons, never deviating by more than 13 points of batting average, seven RBI, eight runs or two games in any individual year. He's the epitome of the "very good, though not elite" outfielder, but that's still a fine early-round pick in any format.

name: Christian Walker
season_outlook: Outside of an oblique strain that cost him five weeks late last season, Walker has been an almost spot-on, 30-HR, 90-RBI, top-eight fantasy first baseman across the past three years. His combination of power, patience and strong defense makes him one of the on-field game's most reliable first basemen, and one of fantasy's most consistent at the position. During the offseason, Walker signed with the Astros, where Daikin Park's Crawford Boxes should prove an enticing target for his pull-oriented swing (64 of his 95 homers from 2022-24 were pulled). Expect similar production from the 34-year-old in 2025.

name: Ivan Herrera
season_outlook: After an encouraging season as a part-time catcher, Herrera appears set to take over as the Cardinals' starter, what with Willson Contreras ticketed for first base in 2025. Herrera sported above-average contact, patience and power metrics as well as solid framing numbers defensively, and he finished with .368/.463/.579 rates while starting 15 of the team's final 32 games. There's enough here to make him a wise No. 2 option for mixed leagues.

name: Lourdes Gurriel Jr.
season_outlook: Gurriel had another productive if unspectacular season at the plate for the Diamondbacks in 2024. He contributes to all five categories, but his batting average is arguably his best contribution to a fantasy team's bottom line. Gurriel has been one of the better contact hitters in baseball in recent seasons, but his aversion to walks limits his ability to reach base. His walk and chase rates were both in the bottom 25th percentile last season and do not show any signs of improvement in the near future. The outfielder is at his best when he is facing southpaws, as he has hit .317/.366/.485 against them over the past two seasons compared to .250/.294/.434 against righties.  The retooled lineup in Arizona could have Gurriel hitting cleanup this season which would allow him to potentially drive in 85 runs for the first time in his career. However, some of the leading indicators around his quality of contact trended in a concerning direction in 2024.

name: Spencer Steer
season_outlook: Steer experienced a down year in 2024, though his skills weren't far off from the previous more productive season. He was victimized by the baseball not carrying as well. Steer's flyball exit velocity was nearly the same as 2023, but the average distance dropped seven feet, costing him homers and BABIP. Furthermore, his batting average dropped 46 points, but his expected average fell only 17 points. Steer made up for the loss in power with 25 steals in 28 attempts (89% success rate). New Reds' manager Terry Francona gives the green light to players with a high success rate, so Steer should continue to be a quiet source of steals, with a good chance of a power rebound. He's only missed 10 games over the last two seasons, helping accumulate plentiful runs and RBI. Steer is slated to handle left field but could see action at the corner infield spots.

name: Paul Goldschmidt
season_outlook: The aging curve appears to have taken hold with Goldschmidt, as his age-37 season saw him post his worst strikeout, walk and home run rates and the lowest isolated power and batting averages of his 14-year MLB career. He did, however, hit 20 home runs across his final 117 games, while mashing lefties (.295/.366/.473), and the move from Busch Stadium to Yankee Stadium should only help him in terms of park factors. Goldschmidt might have one more top-10 fantasy 1B season left in his bat, though his recent trend makes him a wiser player to target for your mixed-league corner infield position.

name: Michael Busch
season_outlook: Busch, a first-round pick by the Dodgers in 2019, was traded to the Cubs last winter, opening up a path to playing time at the major-league level. Busch took advantage and showed what he's made of with an above-average offensive season at age 26 that included 21 homers and a .775 OPS across 567 plate appearances. Best of all for his 2025 outlook, Busch handled same-side pitching capably, slashing .258/.330/.382 against left-handed pitching. That performance along with his defense at first base, which the Cubs see as Gold Glove caliber, figure to keep Busch in the lineup nearly every day. First base has become rather top heavy in fantasy baseball and Busch makes for a decent fallback option for those that end up waiting at the position.

name: Brandon Lowe
season_outlook: This is the Lowe whose name rhymes with "ow," reflecting his six trips to the IL across the past three seasons alone, for back (three), triceps, knee and oblique issues, totaling 162 missed Rays games. Between the absences, Lowe has continued to show elite-to-top-shelf raw power metrics, and his 5.2% home run rate across the last five seasons leads all second basemen. That ability makes him too good to completely ignore in mixed leagues, though selecting him demands a strong backup plan.

name: Kerry Carpenter
season_outlook: The more growth Carpenter shows in the power departments, the more he seems to further slip into the pit of role-player status. He has improved his contact-quality metrics in both of the last two seasons and in 2024 would have had a top-five Statcast Barrel rate if he had the requisite batted-ball qualifications. Sadly, he has also spent time on the IL in each of the last three seasons, twice for spinal issues, and has a gaping 90-point wOBA split so far in the majors. Carpenter is at a critical stage of his career at age 27, with a chance at developing into one of the game's best power hitters, but also the downside of a mere daily-league matchups dynamo.

name: Alec Burleson
season_outlook: Burleson is coming off a breakout season with the Cardinals in which he hit 21 homers with a team-leading 78 RBI. After making a lone, solitary start against a lefty pitcher in 2023, Burleson made 26 starts against left-handed pitching last season, though he managed just a .514 OPS and three of his 21 homers in 142 total plate appearances against southpaws. With that, he is a candidate for a reduction in playing time, and either way the steals are likely unsustainable given his limited sprint speed. Still, Burleson should be able to do enough damage with the platoon edge to be a worthwhile fourth or fifth outfielder in fantasy, especially if he continues to see most of his time in the two hole for St. Louis. The 26-year-old qualifies at first base in addition to outfield in leagues with a 15-game minimum for eligibility.

name: Keibert Ruiz
season_outlook: Ruiz had a bout with the flu early on last season which cost him multiple weeks and caused him to lose nearly 20 pounds. In the end, his OPS fell by nearly 100 points from 2023, though he rebounded a bit in the second half, and it's fair to wonder how much the influenza and subsequent weight loss affected his play. Part of the Nationals' return from the Dodgers in the 2021 Trea Turner-Max Scherzer trade, Ruiz has not quite developed as expected, offensively or defensively. Ruiz makes consistent contact at the plate and packs some power, but a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Signed to a long-term extension in March of 2023, Ruiz will have every chance to rebound and continue his maturation as a player, but at 26 years old, the clock is ticking for him to prove he can make it as a No. 1 catcher.

name: Jackson Holliday
season_outlook: His first taste of the majors was just 21 months after he was selected No. 1 overall in the 2022 amateur draft, but Holliday flopped in what became only a 10-game audition for the Orioles (.059 BA, 18 K's in 34 AB). . He was returned to Triple-A ball and rendered a relative afterthought for the next three months. But, as is often the case with blue-chip prospects, he returned to homer in five of his next 10 games while posting top-shelf raw speed metrics and what would have been a 73rd percentile hard hit rate if he had the requisite at-bats to qualify. Holliday's skills still point to him being a future fantasy superstar and, as a 21-year-old, he remains a dynasty building block. He's projected to be the team's starting second baseman in 2025. With a strong spring, he'll be a high upside mid-to-late rounder -- even in redraft formats.

name: Jonathan India
season_outlook: After a pair of injury-plagued seasons, India appeared in a career-high 151 games last season. His production fell short of his 2021 NL Rookie of the Year effort, but it was a marked improvement over the previous two campaigns. He set personal bests in strikeout and walk rates, fueling the rebound. India needs to make frequent contact since his quality of contact metrics are well below average. He sports below average power, though playing his first four seasons in Great American Ballpark helped him clear double digit homers each year. He'll be challenged to match that power now that he'll play half of his games in cavernous Kauffman Stadium, though his new home digs should help increase his BABIP, so overall production won't suffer too much. The Reds stole 73 more bases than the Royals last season, but India's 87% success rate (27-for-31) over the past two years should keep him active on the basepaths. With his high on base rate, India is ideally suited for points leagues.

name: J.T. Realmuto
season_outlook: The top catcher in all of fantasy baseball not long ago, Realmuto has fallen back to the pack entering 2025. He underwent surgery on his right knee in June and missed five weeks, which kept him under 100 games played last season. The big problem, presumably related to the knee, is that he went from 16 steals in 2023 to a mere two last year. He can still hit for impressive pop, but speed from the catcher position was such a big part of his appeal previously, and while that aspect of his game may not be completely gone, it figures to be diminished in his mid-30s. Further, his walk rate has dipped in recent years, taking his on-base percentage along with it, and Realmuto has slid down the Phillies' order as a result.

name: Matt McLain
season_outlook: Oblique, shoulder and rib injuries cost him the final month of 2023 and the entirety of 2024, but McLain returned to action during the Arizona Fall League and delivered .240/.356/.520 rates while seeing time at three different positions (2B, 3B and CF). He'll be ready to compete for a utility role this spring and, with a strong March, should be ready to pick up where he last left off -- as a potential 25/25 player. McLain does have a lot of swing-and-miss in his game, putting him at risk for slumps and a low batting average, but he's an attractive mid-round pick, with slightly more appeal in rotisserie than points-based leagues.

name: Max Muncy
season_outlook: An oblique strain put Muncy on the shelf in May and eventually forced a move to the 60-day injured list since he was slow to progress. He finally made it back in August and was a regular in the lineup throughout the Dodgers' run to the World Series, doing typical Muncy things with a .163 average but also three homers and 15 walks in the postseason. At 34 years old, Muncy is well established as a low-average, high-OBP slugger from the left side. Given the depth in Los Angeles and his splits in recent years, it seems likely that he will remain limited to a platoon, starting primarily against right-handed pitching. That in theory limits his upside, but Muncy's immense power and the lineup around him make him a potential option at third base or corner infield once the everyday players are off the board.

name: Adolis Garcia
season_outlook: Garcia's 2024 season was a massive step backward after he was an All-Star in two of the previous three years. His slugging percentage was down more than 100 points from 2023 while his .284 OBP was sixth worst among qualified hitters. Garcia still reached 25 homers and 11 steals, though his offensive struggles combined with poor marks on defense could threaten his playing time in 2025. The Rangers figure to give Garcia every chance to bounce back, but the pressure will be on for the 32-year-old to produce at a high level given his limited defensive utility. Garcia missed the end of last season with a knee injury, but surgery was deemed unnecessary and he is expected to enter spring training without limitations.

name: Ceddanne Rafaela
season_outlook: Rafael moved all around the diamond for Boston last season, making 87 appearances in center field, 82 at shortstop, 10 at second base, four at third base and one in right field. However, the Red Sox have since indicated that they believe the lack of a set defensive home may have had an adverse effect on Rafaela's offensive production, which was well below league average. He was briefly the talk of the fantasy baseball world in spring training, but Rafaela's success did not carry over into the regular season, as he fell in the bottom five among qualified hitters in OBP. Through it all, he totaled 15 homers and 19 steals in 152 games, which is impressive for a 23-year-old, even if it was largely volume driven. Center field will be Rafaela's set position for the foreseeable future and the Red Sox will be hoping he can settle in and finds his groove at the plate in 2025.

name: Jake Cronenworth
season_outlook: An All-Star in 2021 and 2022, Cronenworth fractured his right wrist in August of 2023 which brought to an end to a disappointing campaign. He appeared headed for a rebound season in 2024, posting a .753 OPS in the first half before dipping back to .650 after the break. It would be incorrect to label him a slap hitter, but Cronenworth's slugging percentage has fallen below .400 each of the last three years. He may be best suited as a true utility man, but there is little on the Padres' roster standing in his way of reaching 600 plate yet again. Best of all for fantasy purposes, Cronenworth retains eligibility at first base and second base entering his age-31 season, giving him unique and valuable flexibility, especially in leagues with corner and middle spots.

name: Sal Frelick
season_outlook: Frelick's versatility may be his best asset. He played all three outfield positions last season and made enough of an impression in his limited time at third base that manager Pat Murphy has already stated Frelick will get a chance to compete for that spot this spring. It would be a highly unusual profile at third base because Frelick has a fraction of the pop of even an average third baseman these days. Frelick's fantasy value is anchored to his speed and ability to score runs. He is also not going to see much action against lefty starters, so repeating 500-plus plate appearances is a challenge on paper. Murphy's lead foot with the running game is the ultimate draw with Frelick since we know he is going to run when he reaches base. Fantasy managers simply must have the right roster build to add this empty speed in the endgame.

name: Wilyer Abreu
season_outlook: Abreu's impressive minor-league performances in 2022 and 203 got him on some radars, and his first full season of big-league play had its moments. Abreu didn't steal bases like he did in 2022 when he stole 31 bags in Double-A nor did he reach base at a .390 clip as he did between Triple-A and the majors in 2023, but Abreu was a monster against righties, slashing .266/.334/.491 with 14 of his 15 homers. His production against righties was 26 percent above league average, but that all changed against southpaws. His struggles against left-handed pitching are why the likes of Rob Refsnyder persists on the Boston depth chart as the duo make a solid tandem while the club tries to figure out whether Abreu can handle lefties or is destined for a strong-side platoon future like many lefties before him.

name: Luis Garcia Jr.
season_outlook: Garcia is coming off a career year in his ninth season in the organization since he signed as an amateur free agent in 2016. He earned the full-time spot at second base and hit all over the lineup over the course of the season. His lack of patience at the plate makes him better suited for the bottom half of the lineup, and as the Nationals continue to deepen their roster, it will become tougher for Garcia to get out of the lower half of the order unless some skills change. The good news is that he enjoyed his time down there last season, stealing 22 bases in 27 attempts despite just average speed since manager Dave Martinez has a lead foot on the running game. Garcia hit especially well at Nationals Park, slashing .329/.369/.549 with 14 homers at home compared to .233/.265/.335 with four homers on the road.

name: Andres Gimenez
season_outlook: The 2022 version of Gimenez would have been an outstanding fit for Toronto because that version of Gimenez provided one thing absent in most of the Toronto lineups that year -- on-base percentage. Gimenez reached base 37 percent of the time that season while the collective group who hit leadoff for the Jays in 2024 had a .297 on-base percentage. Alas, Gimenez has not come close to replicating that career year from 2022. Gimenez is an impatient hitter who is looking to put the best pitch possible into play and leverage his speed on the basepaths. He has the seventh-fewest walks among all hitters with at least 1500 plate appearances since 2022, but he is also ninth overall among that same group in steal attempts. That's the skill Toronto will be leaning on in 2025 to help bolster the bottom of the lineup.

name: Austin Wells
season_outlook: Wells began 2024 in a timeshare, then emerged as the Yankees' primary backstop. He does not light up his Statcast page, sporting average batted ball skills, but they often improve with young catchers. Wells' high flyball rate supports a solid power floor, but his platoon splits suggest sitting versus southpaws as all 13 of his homers came against right-handers. Strong defense and framing offer leeway to stay in the lineup and improve against southpaws, especially since there is little competition behind the plate in the Bronx after the trade of Jose Trevino to the Reds. Wells' solid plate skills generate a draftable floor, and there are several paths for more production, hence fantasy upside.

name: Gabriel Moreno
season_outlook: Moreno is making good on his prospect promise, though injuries limited him to just 97 games last season. At 24 years old, Moreno improved his strikeout and walk rates, showcasing a highly advanced plate approach. He still lost nearly 20 points of batting average, and the catcher finished with a mere five home runs in 351 plate appearances. With a career groundball rate over 50 percent, Moreno's power upside would seem capped, though one can't help but wonder if there is potential for more since he's such a talented hitter. Perhaps the strongest selling point here is his defense, which earned him a Gold Glove in 2023 and should keep him in the primary role behind the plate in Arizona. Beware that there could be another manager lurking in the weeds waiting to draft Moreno at the end in one-catcher leagues.

name: Cedric Mullins
season_outlook: Mullins has faded into the background a bit over the past few years as young stars like Gunnar Henderson and Adley Rutschman have emerged in Baltimore, but the speedy outfielder continues to produce useful numbers for fantasy managers. Chances are, Mullins will never hit 30 home runs again like he did during his breakout 2021 campaign, but Mullins has launched at least 15 homers each of the past three seasons, providing enough power to complement his speed and keep him viable in mixed leagues. A batting average in the .230s has hurt over the past two seasons, and his playing time against lefties only continues to trend downward, but Mullins' floor against right-handed pitching looks fairly sturdy. He will make over $8 million in his final year of arbitration eligibility.

name: Anthony Volpe
season_outlook: Volpe's sophomore season reflected only minimal growth, mostly in the form of his contact rate. Almost every other underlying metric regressed, with the primary reasons for his improving from SS29 to SS17 (both on the Player Rater and in fantasy points scored) coming from his gains in both runs scored and steals. Volpe will need to either boost his ground-ball rate or his contact quality metrics -- and preferably both -- in order to move much further up the ranks, though the Yankees remain committed to him as their starting shortstop. They might even give him more looks from the leadoff spot, should he continue his contact gains or restore his 2023 level of patience, which would further fill those two important rotisserie departments. Consider him to be a solid mixed-league middle infielder.

name: Masyn Winn
season_outlook: Winn drew criticism from fans and fellow players when he threw 100 mph across the diamond in the 2022 Futures Game, but he's no mere gimmick at the shortstop position. Indeed it is thanks largely to his throwing arm and defense that has he has been able to establish himself as an everyday player in St. Louis. Winn also showed impressive growth at the plate last season, posting 15 homers, 11 steals and a .730 OPS across 637 plate appearances at 22 years old after struggling mightily in his first exposure to major-league pitching in 2023. The batted-ball profile does little to excite, but Winn's speed and contact abilities pushed him into the leadoff spot under manager Oliver Marmol and Winn remained there through the end of last season. Winn said over the winter that he is aiming to steal 30-to-40 bases in 2025, which should be taken with a huge grain of salt, but it's nice to know the intent is there.

name: TJ Friedl
season_outlook: Friedl was limited to just 85 games last season due to a litany of injuries, beginning with a fractured his wrist in spring training. He also missed time with fractured left thumb and hamstring injury. Since 2022, the lefty-swinging Friedl demonstrated reverse splits, though 82% of his action has been facing right-handers. His Hard Hit and Barrel Rates are among the lowest in MLB, but a 45% flyball level yields power and a 15.2% strikeout rate usually keeps his batting average afloat. Last season's .226 average was deflated with an unlucky .229 BABIP. Friedl's defense is below average, so he needs to hit to play. He's ticketed to hold down the busier side of a right field platoon with Austin Hays, but if Friedl struggles, Hays can cut into Friedl's playing time.

name: Mark Vientos
season_outlook: After Brett Baty struggled and was returned to Triple-A, Vientos flourished as the Mets' regular third baseman across the season's final four months. He posted upper-tier raw power metrics while slashing more than 8% off his ground-ball rate, and his 24 homers from June 1 forward ranked fourth-best among third basemen and 12th-best in the majors. Still, Vientos' contact left a lot to be desired, as his 31.2% strikeout rate was seventh-worst over that same time span, which puts him at risk of lengthy cold spells and a low cumulative batting average. He's a legitimate power source with more rotisserie than points-based appeal, but be forewarned that he could be due for some regression in 2025.

name: Heliot Ramos
season_outlook: A top prospect in his earlier seasons as a pro, Ramos' star sagged slightly before he burst onto the scene for the Giants with 20 homers across the final four months of 2024. His mastery of Triple-A ball across the prior year-plus earned him regular at-bats following Michael Conforto's injury in May, and Ramos flashed elite raw power metrics and well above-average speed. That did come with a wide platoon split (198 points of wOBA), a potential advantage to tuck away in ESPN's daily-transactions standard, but Ramos did show enough success against right-handers in the minors that he should take a step forward in 2025. Consider him to be a mid-to-late round pick in larger mixed leagues.

name: Zach Neto
season_outlook: Neto broke out last season to the tune of 23 homers and 30 steals in 155 games for the Angels. Despite that, the fantasy world is treating the shortstop with some trepidation entering his age-24 season in 2025. Most pertinently, his availability for the start of the upcoming season is uncertain after he underwent right shoulder surgery in November. Neto was also caught stealing 10 times and managed just a .697 OPS against right-handed pitching. The concerns are valid, but Neto improved his OBP and SLG significantly in the second half and his playing time will be locked in once he completes his recovery from surgery. His batted-ball profile leaves a lot to be desired, but this kind of power-speed combo is tough to find outside of the early rounds, even if it is largely volume driven.

name: Logan O'Hoppe
season_outlook: O'Hoppe struck out nearly 30 percent of the time last season, but overall he was a bright spot for a last-place Angels squad, hitting 20 homers and providing plus value behind the plate. After missing a large chunk of 2023 with a shoulder injury, O'Hoppe seemed to hit a wall in August of last season, posting a .339 OPS that month before rebounding to .791 in September. Drafted in the 23rd round out of high school in 2018, O'Hoppe has proven to be a tremendous find and developmental success story for the organization. The strikeouts should be manageable with his batted-ball profile, and improvement against left-handed pitching seems likely given his 2023 numbers. Entering his age-25 season, O'Hoppe appears capable of jumping a tier or two at the catcher position while playing his home games at a park that is generally favorable for right-handed power.

name: Lars Nootbaar
season_outlook: It is perplexing to look at Nootbaar's production over three full seasons because we are left wanting more. His strikeout and walk rates are better than average and all measures shows he makes quality contact with the baseball. Yet, Nootbaar has never hit more than 14 homers in a season and has yet to drive in 50 runs in a season. This speaks to Nootbaar's biggest weakness: staying on the field. He and the injured list have been thick as thieves and 2024 saw them spend time together due to a rib fracture and an oblique injury. Nootbaar would be a great fit for higher in the lineup with another team, but St. Louis projects him to hit in the lower half as things stand right now. Maybe this will be the year Nootbaar stays healthy and stays in the lineup enough to put up the type of numbers his overall profile suggests are hiding somewhere, but history says otherwise.

name: Royce Lewis
season_outlook: One of the game's highest risk/reward players, Lewis has missed more Twins games over the past two seasons (172) than he has played during his three-year MLB career, yet in those 152 games played he has 33 HR and 104 RBI. He's still only 25 years old, with plenty of career left in which to shake his growing reputation for being injury prone, but at the same time, fellow Twin Byron Buxton had a similar penchant for absences that he was never able to shake. Lewis certainly possesses the ability to be one of the best at his position, but drafting him requires a leap of faith.

name: Jake Burger
season_outlook: Following a December trade from Miami to Texas, Burger is projected to open the 2025 season as the Rangers' primary first baseman, replacing Nathaniel Lowe. Burger totaled 579 plate appearances last season around an early stint on the injured list with an intercostal strain, falling one home run short of reaching 30 for the second straight year. He has had to deal with a lot in his young career, including two tears of his left Achilles' tendon during his time in the minors, along with a pair of trades. While he's a rather one-dimensional player, Burger hits for enough average -- exactly .250 the last three seasons -- to complement the power and make him worthwhile in traditional fantasy formats. Those in OBP leagues will likely want to downgrade Burger given that he's allergic to walks (career 5.7 percent).

name: Brenton Doyle
season_outlook: After impressing with his glove in 2023, Doyle broke out as a hitter, joining 19 others in the 20/20 club and one of 10 with 20 HR and 30 SB. His breakout was fueled by a 10-point reduction in strikeout rate (down to 25.4%) while increasing his Hard-Hit rate from the 19th to 58th percentile. The power surge wasn't all Coors Field with 11 of his 23 homers coming on the road, though Doyle's .900 home OPS was much better than his .636 road mark. Trusting a one-year breakout is risky, but Doyle is a standout defender with a stolen base floor and Coors Field at his back.

name: Triston Casas
season_outlook: Casas' combination of power and patience makes him a perennial breakthrough candidate, but through three MLB seasons, he has had difficulty staying on the field. An ankle issue cost him two months of 2022, delaying his arrival in Boston, shoulder inflammation prematurely ended his 2023, and torn cartilage in his rib cage shelved him for more than three months of 2024. Casas was also the subject of winter trade rumors, though he'll begin 2025 again as Boston's first baseman, hoping for better luck in the health department. At his best, he could challenge for top-five positional status in any fantasy league.

name: Xavier Edwards
season_outlook: Edwards began the season on the 60-day injured list with a bacterial infection in his left foot. After recovering and spending some time with Triple-A Jacksonville, he was called up and took over as the Marlins' regular shortstop. With some of the worst quality of contact metrics in the league, Edwards depends on a low strikeout rate and a high groundball rate to yield a high batting average. His career .245 xBA suggests regression is coming, but Edwards' speed should allow him to overachieve his estimators. Power, on the other hand, is non-existent. Edwards' fantasy valued is driven by stolen bases, but he'll be challenged to match last season's pace with a likely drop in OBP. His defense is subpar, but the Marlins appear committed to playing him every day.

name: Tyler Stephenson
season_outlook: Stephenson's 1032 plate appearances over the past two seasons are the seventh highest among catchers. Last season, his skills improved over the previous year as he fanned less while increasing his Hard-Hit and Barrel rates, which helped result in a career-high 19 home runs. He also lofted more fly balls, fueling a career-high ISO. Stephenson outpointed his expected stats, some of which is due to playing in Great American Ballpark, but he'll still be challenged to match last season's production. Stephenson's defense remains subpar, though his framing improved, so he should remain the bell cow even with Jose Trevino signed to be his understudy.

name: Ryan O'Hearn
season_outlook: O'Hearn has flourished on the busier side of a platoon, mashing 28 of 30 homers since 2022, and all 15 last season versus right-handers. When he didn't start, O'Hearn usually pinch hit, so he garnered more playing time than a typical lefty platoon batter. Last season, O'Hearn's strikeout rate dropped to a career low 14.0% mark, but his Hard-Hit rate fell precipitously, so he ended up with a 119 wRC+, just a point higher than 2023. There are sexier players with a higher ceiling, but O'Hearn provides a stable floor, embellished by hitting in the middle of a potent lineup. Dual first base and outfield eligibility add to his streaming allure.

name: JJ Bleday
season_outlook: Bleday has had the burden of being a top prospect hanging around him for a while, so it was good to see him finally post a season with the type of production that was once expected of him. Bleday finally got everyday playing time and made the most of it with 20 homers and career bests across the board. The batting average would have been higher had Bleday spent his time solely in a strong-side platoon role, as his .216/.266/.448 line against lefties paled in comparison to his .250/.338/.434 line against righties. He earned his spot in the upper third of the lineup and should remain there as the lefty to split up Brent Rooker and Shea Langeliers in the order against right-handed pitching. A big part of Bleday's growth last year was how he handled fastballs as he raised his batting average against them by 75 points while reducing his whiff rate by 10 percentage points.

name: Willi Castro
season_outlook: Castro has carved out a highly valuable role as a super utilityman with the Twins, perfect for a natural shortstop with plus athleticism. The stolen bases rendering so him so useful in 2023 declined to 14 thefts last year, but additional playing time between five positions allowed Castro to maintain status as a fantasy asset. There are signs of progress with noticeable increases in exit velocity and Hard Hit, fueling a career-high of 47 extra-base hits. Four position eligibility adds to his allure, though he isn't assured of a starting job. Second base is his best opportunity, but even if he remains in a reserve capacity, Castro can be helpful, especially in daily leagues.

name: Matt Shaw
season_outlook: Shaw, the Cubs' first-round pick in the 2023 amateur draft, enters 2025 as a strong candidate to start at third base on Opening Day. After setting Maryland's all-time home run record (53), he managed .357/.400/.618 rates, eight homers and 15 steals across 38 minor league games in his pro debut, then followed it up with a 21-HR, 31-SB 2024 in which he acclimated himself well in 35 season-ending games of Triple-A ball. Shaw's well-rounded skill set appeals to any fantasy format and, while his speed might be his most bankable immediate tool, he could quickly develop in the power department. He's a dynasty building block and a late-round flier, even in ESPN standard redraft leagues.

name: Dylan Crews
season_outlook: A cornerstone of the Nationals' rebuild, Crews, the No. 2 overall pick of the 2023 draft, has all of the tools necessary to develop into an eventual rotisserie and points-based fantasy star. His contact-oriented swing and blazing speed were most apparent during his 2024 MLB debut (albeit more rewarded in roto formats), but his contact quality metrics bodes well for his eventually adding enough power to help more in points leagues. Crews will need to curb his 56.4% ground ball rate in order to truly break through, but he's off to a good start to his career. He warrants a mid-round selection in redraft leagues and is a near-building block selection in dynasty formats.

name: Nathaniel Lowe
season_outlook: After acquiring Jake Burger from the Marlins in December, the Rangers traded Lowe to Washington, where he will begin a new chapter in 2025. Lowe began last season on the injured list with an oblique strain and missed 22 games after missing a total of 11 games over the prior three seasons. He won the Silver Slugger at first base in 2022 when he hit .302 with 27 homers, and while Lowe has not come close to replicating that level of production since, he's been rather consistent, with his OPS marks falling within a narrow range between .762 and .775 in his other three full MLB seasons. Similar rate numbers can be expected in 2025, and with the everyday playing time afforded by his glove and on-base skills, Lowe could very well reach 20 homers for just the second time in his career.

name: Luis Robert Jr.
season_outlook: Robert strained his hip flexor a week into the 2024 season and missed close to two months as a result. The outfielder struck out in nearly one-third of his 425 plate appearances last season and his power completely evaporated down the stretch, as Robert didn't hit a single homer in September and only popped three home runs in total after the All-Star break. It appears Robert, 27, will be given a chance to rebuild his value and audition for other teams as an everyday player on the South Side to begin 2025, and he had 38 homers and 20 steals as recently as 2023. The injury history and shaky plate discipline give him a wider range of outcomes than most, but Robert is an impressive athlete with obvious bounce-back potential.

name: Ezequiel Tovar
season_outlook: A 60th percentile Barrel Rate and 46th percentile Hard-Hit rate aren't eye-popping, but they're adequate when you play half of your games in Coors Field and helped result in 26 homers. Even so, Tovar's home OPS was just 19 points better than his road mark. A career 28% strikeout rate is troubling, as is a low 3.7% walk rate, and both limit his potential for run production. At just 23 years old, Tovar has time to translate his strong hand-eye coordination into more contact. Gold glove defense will keep Tovar in the lineup, though until he makes better swing decisions, he's best deployed in favorable matchups.

name: Jasson Dominguez
season_outlook: ?The Martian? figures to take over starting left field duties for the Yankees in 2025 and, while his defense often came into question during a late-season audition last year, his Triple-A dominance in 2023-24 (.325/.391/.495 rates, 7 HR, 18 SB in 53 games) reflects his immense offensive potential. Dominguez is one of the more important hitters to watch during spring training, as more patience and more lift in his swing than he showed in his two cups of coffee with the Yankees could do him a world of good. He should be a good source of stolen bases at the very least, a back-of-the-roster mixed-league player at the median, and a breakthrough player with building-block dynasty potential at his best.

name: Daulton Varsho
season_outlook: Once earmarked to be a bat-first catcher, Varsho is now a Gold Glove outfielder with declining hitting skills. His barrel rate has fallen two straight seasons while his flyball percentage has skyrocketed. Varsho's strikeout rate is also climbing. He's hitting too many flyballs, many with such a high launch angle that they don't have the carry to leave the yard. Furthermore, he needed shoulder surgery, which often saps power and could delay his 2025 debut. Varsho was once a trendy name when he still had catcher eligibility, but in the outfield, he gets lost in the shuffle. Simply put, there are more reliable sources for cheap power and speed.

name: Andrew Vaughn
season_outlook: Vaughn is one of just 12 first-base-eligible players to have logged at least 550 plate appearances in each of the past three seasons. There is value in volume, but how much actual production Vaughn will bring to the table is debatable with all the uncertainty surrounding the Chicago roster. There have been rumors of them dealing Luis Robert, which could affect Vaughn's already limited RBI chances. Vaughn has not embraced the heavy pull tendencies that most corner sluggers do which has put a cap on any projected home-run total despite his ability to make better-than-average contact. Vaughn is projected to hit cleanup for the White Sox and there is little reason to think he won't turn in similar counting stats since his profile has been remarkably stable for a young hitter to date. He simply lacks the power profile that most chase at the first base position.

name: Francisco Alvarez
season_outlook: Coming off a 25-HR (albeit one-dimensional) rookie season in 2023, Alvarez continued to struggle with strikeouts and a high ground ball rate last year, while also missing nearly two months due to April surgery on his thumb. At times, he continued to flash the immense power potential that could eventually make him a positional leader in the home run department, but -- as is often the case with young catchers (he's 23) -- he continued to struggle with the often lengthy adjustment curve to the majors. Alvarez's youth warrants patience as he gets comfortable with the bat and, as the starting catcher for a potent Mets offense, he's one of the better breakthrough candidates at the position. A strong spring would go a long way towards earning him upper-tier draft status in mixed leagues.

name: Spencer Horwitz
season_outlook: Twice traded during a 24-hour period in December, Horwitz is more of a fantasy "Swiss army knife" than a hot potato. Eligible at both first and second base, he brought a sound plate approach and decent pop while serving in a starting role for the Blue Jays across the final three-plus months of 2024. Horwitz figures to be the Pirates' regular first baseman this season, where his skill set should make him a high-floor fantasy pick in the later rounds of drafts, particularly in points-based or sabermetric formats.

name: Jeff McNeil
season_outlook: The past couple years have been tough for McNeil, a former batting champion, as his production has become voluminous oatmeal that does the job but is nobody's first choice for sustenance. While the run production has still been useful, there are no signs of a substantial rebound in batting average as McNeil moves into his mid-30s. He remains one of the higher contact hitters in the league but his ability to generate consistent quality contact has waned in recent seasons. Heading into 2025, McNeil appears likely to spend another year in the bottom third of the Mets' lineup.

name: J.P. Crawford
season_outlook: Crawford was coming off a 2023 season in which he smacked a career-best 19 homers with a .380 on-base percentage, fueled by his best walk rate in a full season and leading to nearly 100 runs scored. Last season, a fractured pinky was an issue in the middle of the summer, but Crawford was only hitting .204/.296/.347 with a 22.8 percent strikeout rate prior to the injury. He returned at the end of August but finished with a .194/.319/.245 line the rest of the way. Perhaps the lesson learned here is what goes up must come down, but Crawford had never struggled to this level since his first season in Seattle back in 2019. The challenge with Crawford is he does not have a single fantasy skill to bank on, so he either rebounds by batted-ball fortune and moves back up the lineup or hits ninth and lives on the waiver wire.

name: Nolan Schanuel
season_outlook: Schanuel famously debuted in the majors a little over a month after being drafted with the 11th overall pick in 2023, as the Angels did away with the typical prospect development path and tried desperately to remain competitive in Shohei Ohtani's final year under contract. Schanuel has performed admirably since then, especially for a player that was thrown into the deep end, batting .255 with a .354 OBP in 176 MLB games to date. He has slugged just .357 in that span, however, and managed just 13 home runs in 607 plate appearances last season. That lack of power makes Schanuel a tough fit at first base, a position known for power, though in fantasy leagues with a designated corner infield spot, Schanuel could be passable. He wouldn't seem to have much performance downside, at least, given the plate skills he has shown through age 22.

name: Josh Jung
season_outlook: There was much expected of Jung after his smashing debut in 2023, but his 2024 never really got off the ground since Jung dealt with wrist troubles all season. He initially fractured his wrist the first week of the season after being hit by a pitch. Jung then missed over 100 games and rushed his rehab to get back to the club in July, only to wind up back on the IL three weeks later. Jung went on to have a second wrist surgery to relieve the pain he was still experiencing, but is expected to be 100 percent by the time camp starts in Arizona. It's been encouraging to see Jung's strikeout rate improve each season he has been in the big leagues, but the next step will be to accept more walks because he has been one of the more impatient hitters in the league, preferring to press the action rather than letting the action come to him. Jung is projected to hit in the bottom half of the retooled Texas lineup this season but could work his way up over the course of the year.

name: Josh Lowe
season_outlook: Lowe appeared in only 106 games last season as a hamstring issue delayed his debut until early May, and then he was subsequently sidelined with an oblique injury. Lowe appeared overly aggressive at times, swinging at pitches outside the strike zone, and yet he was too passive in the zone, resulting in a high 31.8 percent strikeout rate. If Lowe can improve his approach, he can take advantage of barrel and hard-hit rates in the 70th percentile, along with a 94 percent career success rate on stolen bases (61-for-65). Roster the steals, and hope for better swing decisions in 2025.

name: Tyler O'Neill
season_outlook: O'Neill will begin a new chapter with the Orioles in 2025 after signing a three-year deal in December. While Baltimore has an up-and-coming young team, it may not have been able to entice O'Neill without the changes to the left-field at Camden Yards, which has been a nightmare for right-handed power hitters over the past three seasons. O'Neill spent the 2024 campaign with Boston after six seasons in St. Louis, and he rejuvenated his career with the Red Sox, reaching 30 homers for the second time. After a couple seasons with 14-plus steals, O'Neill's running has declined over the past two years, which is probably a good thing given the outfielder's injury history. As he approaches his 30th birthday in June, O'Neill continues to struggle with strikeouts, but he blisters the ball when he makes contact.

name: Austin Hays
season_outlook: Hays split last season between Philadelphia and Baltimore, finishing with an underwhelming .255/.303/.396 slash line in 85 games. The veteran outfielder was an All-Star in 2023, but his .569 OPS against right-handed pitching doomed him last year. Hays excelled versus lefties, however, with a 354/.405/.537 slash line in 90 plate appearances, setting him up for a platoon role in 2025. Landing in Cincinnati on a one-year deal is favorable and could make him a plus option for streaming purposes. There's an outside chance he rediscovers his prior for and takes playing time in right field from TJ Friedl, who should see most of the action against right-handers.

name: Ha-Seong Kim
season_outlook: October shoulder surgery is expected to keep Kim on the IL for the onset of 2025, which could explain how it took until early February for him to find work. The Rays plan for him to take over as their regular shortstop once healthy, after which point his past excellence in terms of contact, patience and raw speed might make him a top-10 rotisserie player at the position. Kim is a player probably best targeted via midseason trade than stashed on draft day, but he's still worth mixed-league middle infield consideration despite the injury questions he'll initially face.

name: Colton Cowser
season_outlook: Though he disappointed during a 2023 cup of coffee, Cowser quickly emerged as a bona fide MLB regular in the early stages of his rookie 2024, swatting six homers across an 11-game stretch in April to effectively lock himself into a starting role (131-of-153 Orioles games) the rest of the way. His power metrics were all well above-average, though his penchant for strikeouts threatens streakiness and a low batting average in 2025. Cowser should again serve as the team's starting left fielder and a heart-of-the-order bat -- a good place to be in a lineup chock full of long-term upside. He's a mid-to-late round value.

name: Brooks Lee
season_outlook: Kiley McDaniel's No. 29 overall prospect entering last season, Lee fell well short of expectations during his rookie campaign, hampered by back and biceps injuries while posting mediocre-at-best contact quality metrics. He'll be in the mix for the Twins' second base job in the best-case scenario, a utility role at his median, and a fill-in role behind the team's many injury-prone infielders on the low end. Lee seems most likely to contribute in the batting average category as he matures. He'll need to excel in Grapefruit League play to be anything more than a late-round mixed flier.

name: Sean Murphy
season_outlook: Murphy suffered an oblique injury on Opening Day, missed two months and simply never hit his stride at the plate in 2024. He stayed in the lineup because of the value he provided behind the plate, but his offensive production cratered as his OPS+ went from 127 to 76 in just one season. It is important to remember that Murphy is just a couple years removed from a season in which he exhibited power to all fields and became one of the toughest outs in the league at the catcher position. Admittedly, he produced like a backup catcher last season, but the progress he showed in 2022 and 2023 is enough to warrant giving Murphy another chance. Murphy no longer has Travis d'Arnaud to share playing time with and should see as many starting assignments as his body can handle.

name: Carlos Santana
season_outlook: Even at age 38, Santana continues to be one of the better points-league values in fantasy drafts. He's only the sixth player in history to have managed at least a 10% batting title-eligible walk rate in 14 straight seasons and he's the only active player with at least an 80% contact rate and 800 walks (he has 1,278). That polished plate approach continues to earn Santana regular at-bats, which is what he should receive back in Cleveland, as the Guardians' 1B replacement for Josh Naylor. Even in the waning years of Santana's career, he's a high-floor, mid-to-late round value in mixed leagues.

name: Ryan Jeffers
season_outlook: Jeffers had a strong 2023 season anchored by a career-best .276 average despite the 27.8 percent strikeout rate. He had rediscovered some of his 2022 power and repeated his home-run total from the season prior, but batted-ball fortunes really went his way that year, with a .359 BABIP driving the overall average. This past season, Jeffers reduced his strikeout rate by seven full percentage points, yet his batting average dropped 50 points year over year even as his batted-ball tendencies were nearly identical to 2023. We just don't often see batted-ball fortunes swing this wildly, but the .238 BABIP last year is what ultimately pulled his average down. Positive regression should help get Jeffers back over league average in that regard, but don't bank on 20-plus homers again.

name: Josh Bell
season_outlook: Now 32, the annually streaky Bell is at a dangerous point on his career curve. He's coming off a 2024 during which he posted the worst full-season whiff rate of his career, his lowest average exit velocity since 2017, and his worst hard-hit rate since 2018. Additionally, his defense at first base continued to grade among the league's worst. Nevertheless, the Nationals have brought him back (he was previously there in 2021-22) to serve as their regular DH, recognizing his ability to deliver at least league-average hitting rates from the middle of their lineup. Bell is in a good spot to return mixed-league corner infield value for another year, though his downside is creeping up annually.

name: Christopher Morel
season_outlook: Morel was batting just .199/.302/.373 when the Cubs dealt him to the Rays just before the trade deadline. He performed even worse in the junior circuit, posting a .191/.258/.289 line with Tampa Bay. Morel still managed his second 20-homer season while demonstrating progress with more walks and fewer strikeouts. Morel's poor defense will be hidden in left field, where he's ticketed to play regularly. There's potential for 30 homers if he reverts to his pull-heavy approach from 2023, and eligibility at second base and third base -- with bonus outfield eligibility in leagues with a 10-game minimum -- helps soften the blow of the low average.

name: Colt Keith
season_outlook: Effectively promised an everyday role with the Tigers after he signed a six-year contract in January, Keith had his moments as a rookie in 2024, even if his cumulative numbers appeared quite ordinary. He posted above-average contact, selectivity and raw speed metrics, and across one 52-game stretch around midseason, hit 11 homers with a .244 ISO to hint at prospective growth in that department. Long regarded one of the Tigers' top prospects, Keith should take another step forward in 2025, with a ceiling within the top-10 fantasy second basemen.

name: Jonah Heim
season_outlook: The Rangers have made it clear that the plan is to have an even timeshare behind the plate in 2025, with Heim splitting time equally with Kyle Higashioka, who was brought in on a one-year deal. Heim was an All-Star and won a Gold Glove in 2023, but his performance fell off a cliff last season, both offensively and defensively. His strikeout rate remained right around his career average, but his walk rate dipped, taking his OBP along with it. The quality of contact was also severely lacking, though Heim reached double-digit homers for the fourth consecutive season. He could approach 400 plate appearances even with the arrival of Higashioka to Texas, and Heim has enough power and enough recent success to still be worthy of consideration as a second catcher in two-catcher leagues.

name: Jorge Soler
season_outlook: Soler was moved to the Angels in the offseason, which may allow him to mimic the career path Marcell Ozuna has taken the past two seasons in Atlanta. Soler and Ozuna share a similar profile in that both are known for their hard contact at the plate as well as the hard contact off their iron gloves in the outfield. Ozuna's career resurgence came about once Atlanta threw him in to the full-time designated hitter role and let him flourish, and Soler now has that same opportunity with the Angels that he was never going to have with Atlanta. Soler's strikeout rate has been better in recent seasons, but it's still worse than average, and that combined with his slow speed puts a hard cap on his batting average. Still, the power and run production could be surprisingly useful.

name: Rhys Hoskins
season_outlook: Hoskins' first season away Philadelphia did not exactly go as planned, and the 2023 layoff due to his recovery from ACL surgery certainly did not help matters. The old saying goes, "hitting is timing and pitching is about the disruption of timing," and while Hoskins still got to enjoy familiar National League pitching, the long layoff was a major disruptor of timing. That said, his strikeout rate has ticked up each of the past four seasons, so it's a trend that goes beyond last year. Hoskins has not lost the ability to barrel up a baseball, but his ability to hit fastballs is showing cracks, as his batting average against fastballs has gone from .287 in 2018 down to .241 last season. He will be 32 when the 2025 season begins and will be aiming to rebuild his numbers to the point where his agent advises him to decline his $18 million mutual option for 2026.

name: Ryan McMahon
season_outlook: One of only 12 infielders to hit 20-plus homers in each of the last five complete MLB seasons, McMahon's fantasy value has been plenty buoyed by Coors Field's high altitude. He's a career .265/.340/.474 hitter there, compared to only .220/.306/.367 on the road, giving him matchups appeal in daily leagues but also mixed-league corner infield value from a cumulative standpoint. Forgive McMahon for his ghastly .197/.271/.298 rates and 30.7% strikeout rate across 2024's final two months as he caught an illness shortly before that which caused him to lose 15-20 pounds. There might be rebound value here, with the only pitfall being the slight possibility the Rockies could look to trade him come deadline time.

name: Joey Ortiz
season_outlook: With Willy Adames leaving in free agency, Ortiz appears primed to take over as the primary shortstop for the Brewers in 2025 after playing mostly at third base in his first season with Milwaukee. Ortiz ended up batting just .239 across 511 plate appearances last season, but his OBP was 90 points higher on account of an 11 percent walk rate. The 26-year-old's sprint speed is well above average and he used that speed to steal 11 bases in 2024, though he was also caught stealing six times. He could stand to improve his efficiency on the basepaths, especially if he is to take full advantage of manager Pat Murphy's green light on the running game. The modest power is another problem, but there will be less pressure on Ortiz's bat at shortstop than at third base. His profile fits fine at short, so similar playing-time volume can be expected this season.

name: Luis Rengifo
season_outlook: Rengifo was not in the Opening Day lineup for the Angels last season and ended up making three separate trips to the injured list, which kept him 80 games played. First he dealt with a viral infection that caused painful blisters on his feet, while wrist trouble shelved him on the other two occasions. Despite those issues, Rengifo swiped 24 bags in 31 attempts, showing an entirely new level with his speed after he had previously topped out at six steals in a season. He also hit an even .300 during his time on the field, up close to 40 points from 2023, though it's difficult to fully buy into either new element of his game given the sample size and Rengifo's performance history. That said, Rengifo has more pop than he showed last season, and while he is no longer quad-eligible like he was entering 2024, he still qualifies at third base and second base, providing valuable flexibility.

name: Andrew Benintendi
season_outlook: Benintendi hit 20 homers for the first time since his rookie season, but otherwise he had a disappointing 2024 campaign much like the rest of the White Sox team. Benintendi has seen his batting average drop 75 points since the 2022 season as his performance against lefty pitching has declined. Most recently he hit .207 against lefties. One could look at his downward trend as a pattern and expect worse, or perhaps see 2024 as the outlier of the recent four-year sample and bank on a rebound in his batting average. Benintendi should once again get all the playing time he can handle, mostly because the roster lacks better options, and his .263/.328/.502 slash line from the second half of the season suggests there still might be some life in his bat. However, he has not slugged above .400 in three seasons now which makes his ability to repeat 20 homers questionable.

name: Ryan Mountcastle
season_outlook: Mountcastle slugged 22 home runs at home in 2021 before the Orioles changed the dimensions at Camden Yards. Over the past three seasons, Mountcastle as managed a total of 28 homers at home, but the good news is that the fences are coming back to a happy medium in 2025 between their original dimensions and where they were over the past three years. Mountcastle should once again have a realistic chance of challenging 30 homers rather than needing two seasons to get there. His plate discipline measures continue to be slightly below average, but with regular playing time between first base and DH, Mountcastle should be able to find a level of production somewhere between what he did in 2021 and where he was in 2022.

name: Bo Naylor
season_outlook: Naylor did little to advance his offensive game in 2024, turning in some of the worst contact-quality metrics among MLB regulars, while seeing his ground-ball, whiff and chase rates rise. It wasn't what fantasy managers wanted to see, after he was projected to be a better-than-league average regular at his position. Naylor, now 25, still has time to right the ship, but he'd need to impress during spring training to be looked at as anything more than a speculative No. 2 fantasy backstop in 15-team mixed leagues.

name: Jake McCarthy
season_outlook: McCarthy had a solid 2024 after fighting against the pressures of statistical expectations the previous season. Last season saw McCarthy avoid the demotions to Triple-A Reno and stick with the big-league club while exceeding 20 steals for the third consecutive campaign. The surprise was that he once again hit for average as he had in 2022 when he first appeared as a regular with the club. McCarthy's game is all about his speed and making contact because the quality of his contact is some of the worst in the league by most measures. His slash-and-dash approach works as long as the batted-ball fortunes swing his way, but he still has a minor-league option remaining, so another 2023-like slump could see McCarthy returning to the biggest little city in the world.

name: Lane Thomas
season_outlook: The Nationals surprised many by holding Thomas at the 2023 trade deadline, but as they fell out of contention last season, it seemed increasingly likely that he would get dealt. Thomas was finally moved to Cleveland, and while his numbers with the Guardians down the stretch of the regular season were poor, he turned it on again in the postseason with a couple homers and a .766 OPS across 10 playoff games. Now 29 years old, he enters 2025 atop the depth chart in center field in his final year before free agency. Thomas' 28-homer, 20-steal campaign in 2023 seemed like a career year as it was unfolding and he should not be expected to reach those heights again. That said, there is room for a rebound and the projected playing time gives him a decent floor for cross-category production.

name: Masataka Yoshida
season_outlook: Yoshida had a disappointing sophomore campaign in Boston, mainly due to injury. A thumb sprain cost him nearly seven weeks in the summer, but then he played through a shoulder injury that ultimately required surgery in October. Yoshida could provide some value in 2025 if he is fully recovered, especially considering many fantasy managers are not eager to fill their utility slot on the roster early in drafts, and that is the only place Yoshida is eligible on draft day. Yoshida has already proven he is quite capable of hitting for average with his excellent bat-to-ball skills at the plate. Boston tried to move his contract in the winter, but there are three more years and $54 million left on it, and to date the club has not yet found any takers. Fantasy managers could do a lot worse in the later rounds than taking a chance on a bounce-back season from the 31-year-old.

name: Connor Norby
season_outlook: It looked like Norby might get lost in the shuffle among the Orioles' talented young corps of infielders, but he got the opening he needed with a deadline trade to the Marlins last season. After the move, Norby posted a .760 OPS and seven homers across 162 plate appearances with Miami. Granted he did most of his damage during a particularly hot stretch from late August into September in which he slashed .333/.377/.719 with six homers in just 14 games. A second-round pick in 2021, Norby has struggled with strikeouts at the upper levels, fanning in nearly one-third of his plate appearances as a rookie. Those issues could threaten Norby's spot on the big-league roster, but after what he did down the stretch, the 24-year-old appears penciled in a third base for the Marlins entering spring training.

name: Ke'Bryan Hayes
season_outlook: Many were expecting another step forward for Hayes in 2024 after his strong 2023 campaign in which he set career highs in everything but steals. However, a bothersome back had other plans for Hayes and he eventually succumbed to those issues in mid-August. Hitters absolutely need a healthy core and back in order to drive the baseball. If anything, the fact Hayes had nearly league-average exit velocity despite the back troubles speaks to his natural talent. Hayes could absolutely repeat his 2023 numbers if his back troubles are behind him and he can resume his regular spot in the daily lineup. His overall profile still fits better down in the lineup than it does toward the top, but one should not be judged on the merits of a season riddled with back troubles when we have seen recent success from the same player.

name: Patrick Bailey
season_outlook: Bailey suffered a concussion in early May of 2024 when he was struck in the catcher's mask by a foul ball. He was activated a little over a week later, only to wind up right back on the concussion IL with lingering symptoms. In August, Bailey was sidelined again with an oblique injury. It's rather amazing that despite the fits and starts, he was able to win the Gold Glove at catcher, which speaks to his toughness and resilience at a position that absolutely requires it. Offensively, Bailey mostly struggled, finishing with a .637 OPS and eight homers across 448 plate appearances, though his defense will afford him time to continue developing at the plate. Entering his age-26 season, Bailey still has a ways to go with the bat, but the projected volume puts him firmly in the C2 mix in two-catcher leagues.

name: Parker Meadows
season_outlook: Meadows struggled mightily at the onset of 2024 after earning the Tigers' starting center field job out of spring training, batting .096 with 32 K's in 73 at-bats before ultimately being demoted back to Triple-A. A hamstring strain that cost him roughly a month's time following his July recall further set him back. Meadows did, however, ultimately acclimate himself to the role across his final 47 regular-season and seven postseason games, batting .292/.341/.495 to rekindle enthusiasm for a prospective 2025 breakthrough. His polished plate approach and elite speed should be most appealing to rotisserie managers, who should consider him in the mid-to-late rounds.

name: Jesus Sanchez
season_outlook: Though Sanchez's surface numbers gave the look of a player spinning his wheels, his 2024 actually reflected big strides in terms of contact quality. Statcast had him in the 95th percentile in terms of hard contact, and he did homer 14 times across his final 291 at-bats. His problems with left-handed pitchers (a .233 career wOBA, 105 points beneath his number against righties) are his biggest limitation, and fantasy managers in leagues with daily transactions should tuck that away. Consider Sanchez as a back-of-your-lineup pick in 12-team mixed leagues.

name: Michael Conforto
season_outlook: Conforto returned to the 20-homer level last season for the first time since 2019, and he had a solid .237/.309/.450 slash line in 130 games. An increase in exit velocity and launch angle fueled the power surge. Last year, Conforto faced right-handers 78% of the time (league average is 72%) despite posting an OPS versus lefties 152 points higher than righties. His three-year OPS is a bit better against southpaws, yet he's pigeonholed in a platoon. His xBA in every full season since 2017 is between .243 and .262. He's played his career in pitcher-friendly venues and will continue to do so in Dodgers Stadium after signing a one-year, $17 million deal. Conforto is best used as a daily league streamer.

name: Nick Gonzales
season_outlook: Gonzales, the No. 7 overall pick in the 2020 amateur draft, appears likely to fall significantly short of the scouts' initial projections. Still, he has nevertheless carved out a respectable role for himself for the foreseeable future. The Pirates' probable second baseman, he's good enough in terms of contact and pop to retain a regular role and, as a 25-year-old, he's still young enough to perhaps take another developmental step with the right tweaks to his game. Consider Gonzales to be a volume-oriented deep mixed or NL-only middle infielder.

name: Jordan Walker
season_outlook: It certainly seems like forever ago that Walker hit safely in 12 consecutive games to begin his MLB career, doesn't it? He has generally struggled at this level since, thrice being returned to Triple-A Memphis following slumps, while his strikeout and ground-ball rates trended badly in the wrong direction last year. Frustrated with his own performance, Walker spent the winter working with new Cardinals hitting coach Brant Brown, which perhaps could help rekindle his future fantasy potential. Walker warrants close attention in Grapefruit League play accordingly, and here's hoping that a strong performance will earn him more of a commitment from the Cardinals to grant him regular at-bats. He's young enough to still make big offensive strides, but we'd like to see some evidence of them before regarding him as anything more than a mixed-league dart throw.

name: Connor Wong
season_outlook: Wong was barely on the radar for fantasy players heading into last season. His 2023 season saw him strike out a third of the time and offer little production compared to what he had done as a minor leaguer, both in the Dodgers and Red Sox organizations. However, 2024 was amazing for those who got on board early with Wong's production. He reduced his strikeout rate by 10 percentage points and raised his batting average 45 points in the process. It took until July for Wong to hit below .300 in a month, though things did eventually correct themselves as Wong's .307 first-half batting average fell to .246 in the second half. If the contact gains for Wong are real, it should help him hit for a better average than most catchers. That said, the metrics around his quality of contact do not paint a particularly favorable picture.

name: Joc Pederson
season_outlook: One of baseball's most productive platoon men, Pederson's .371 wOBA against right-handers over the last three seasons combined ranks 14th (among 166 hitters with at least 900 plate appearances against them), while his 52.0% hard-hit rate against them places 12th. Expect the Rangers to use him accordingly in 2025, starting at DH primarily against righties, bolstering his batting ratios and making him especially attractive in ESPN's daily-transactions offerings. Pederson's strengths in his particular role even give him back-of-your-lineup mixed-league appeal from a cumulative stat line perspective.

name: Thairo Estrada
season_outlook: After a miserable 2024 derailed by a wrist injury and cratering contact-quality metrics, Estrada landed in the one place that might well restore any hope of mixed-league value: Coors Field. There, the spacious outfield gaps might help restore enough of his lost batting average to fuel a stolen base boost. Estrada is probably a mere placeholder until Adael Amador is deemed to be MLB ready, but he's at least worth a look in his Coors games until then.

name: Jeimer Candelario
season_outlook: Candelario is your typical mid-range starting corner infielder, which is why the Reds' $32 million commitment to him over the next two seasons is so important to his fantasy valuation -- it promises him extensive looks as one of their regulars. His defense at third base unfortunately regressed last season, but he at least hit 20-plus homers for the second consecutive year and produced .200-plus ISO for the third time in the past five seasons. Expect more of the same from Candelario, whose matchups appeal gets a boost in his home games at HR-friendly Great American Ball Park, but understand that he's more quantity- than quality-driven for fantasy purposes.

name: Tyler Fitzgerald
season_outlook: Fitzgerald was one of 2024's feel-good stories, but Lady Luck was a big factor. His BABIP was bloated, and as a result, his .280 batting average far outpaced his .227 expected mark. Power was driven by a 44.6 percent flyball rate and a high 16.7 percent HR/FB. His barrel rate was only 53rd percentile. Regression is coming, and new president of baseball operations Buster Posey knows it, as he brought in Willy Adames to play shortstop and push Fitzgerald to the keystone where his bat will play better. Fitzgerald was productive in the minors, but he was always old for the level. It may be best to let others pay for last season's exploits.

name: Jesse Winker
season_outlook: Before you get carried away by Winker's 2024 rebound, keep this fact in mind: All 14 of his stolen bases last season came across an 85-game span while with the Nationals. In his other 670 MLB games that surrounded it, he has a grand total of three steals. Winker is better appreciated for his elite plate discipline which is attractive enough in points-based and sabermetric play to even scrape the final rounds of ESPN leagues. For 2025, it's wiser to expect something closer to his 2020-24, per-162-game averages of .252/.362/.424 rates, 21 homers and five stolen bases.

name: Zack Gelof
season_outlook: Athletics fans were optimistic after Gelof's fine rookie season in 2023, but he looked like a freshman in his sophomore season. His 34% strikeout rate was the worst among qualified batters. Gelof especially struggled with breaking balls, and it wasn't long before he was dropped from the two-hole. Even with his contact issues, Gelof produced 17 homers and 25 steals. The Athletics are committed to having Gelof learn on the job, and playing in Sacramento could help spur his offense with a more hitter-friendly park. Ultimately, it's going to come down to Gelof demonstrating better pitch recognition and improving against off-speed and breaking stuff. If you can absorb Gelof's average, he'll be an asset in the other four roto categories.

name: Alex Verdugo
season_outlook: Verdugo lingered on the free agent market deep into the offseason, as teams perhaps began to recognize him as more of a role player than a regular. He has long struggled against same-handed pitchers (.253/.314/.337 career rates against lefties) and, in 2024, didn't capitalize upon Yankee Stadium's lefty-friendly confines, batting a mere .206/.268/.292 with four homers across his final 77 regular-season games. Verdugo would need to find a team willing to promise him a similarly sizable role to be a mixed-league asset, otherwise he's better left to daily-league matchups usage in fantasy formats.

name: Matt Vierling
season_outlook: Vierling brings dual eligibility to the table in 2025, qualifying at third base and the outfield after a season of growth in 2024. He made the most of his everyday time in the Detroit lineup, setting career highs in the run production categories while not sacrificing in other areas to do so. Vierling's best skill is his ability to stay disciplined in the strike zone, and his all-fields approach helps keep his batting average above the league average. His numbers could improve further in 2025, especially if Detroit moves Vierling's bat to the middle of the lineup where he could break up the lefty bats of Riley Greene and Kerry Carpenter in tougher matchups. Vierling also has the potential to help in steals if manager A.J. Hinch removes the restrictor plates on the Detroit running game this season.

name: Jose Miranda
season_outlook: Miranda, Lin-Manuel's cousin, fueled his own celebrity last July, tying a major league record by generating a hit in 12 consecutive at-bats. Unfortunately, back issues landed him on the IL twice thereafter, and he hit just .217 with no homers and only 11 extra-base hits the rest of the way. Miranda has long possessed a strong contact, line drive-oriented approach at the plate, and he figures to be a favorite for the first base role to begin 2025. Injuries have held him back the past two seasons, making him a wiser late-round investment in deeper mixed leagues than something more, but he's a player to watch during Grapefruit League play.

name: Jacob Young
season_outlook: A speedy center fielder with elite defensive skills, Young is a handy placeholder for the rebuilding Nationals, who await Robert Hassell III's big-league arrival to join Dylan Crews and James Wood to give them potentially three elite youngsters in their outfield. Young offers little more beyond above-average contact ability, but the total package is enough to make him a rotisserie-relevant late round pick. He could be one of the cheapest 30-SB candidates you'll find in drafts.

name: MJ Melendez
season_outlook: Across only three MLB seasons, Melendez's fantasy value has gone from a near-top-100 overall player to an almost complete afterthought. Losing catcher eligibility following his disappointing 2023 represented his first significant setback. His regressions in terms of walk, raw-power and chase rates last season sealed the deal as almost-universal fantasy cut. It's hard to fathom Melendez's decline, considering he's still only 26 years old. A crisper approach at the plate might help him restore some of his lost power and on-base ability. That said, he'd need a standout spring to be anything more than a mixed-league dart throw.

name: Luis Campusano
season_outlook: Coming off a promising finish to 2023 (.343/.389/.524 rates across the final two months), Campusano got off to an encouraging start in 2024, batting .283/.323/.442 while starting 30 of the Padres' first 41 games. Unfortunately, a thumb injury suffered shortly thereafter derailed his campaign, as he hit just .208 the rest of the way, posting poor defensive metrics and ultimately slipping into a backup role behind Kyle Higashioka. With Higashioka now in Texas, the Padres should give Campusano another chance to claim the starting role, from which his contact ability would make him a solid mixed league No. 2 catcher. Monitor his positional battle with Elias Diaz.
